publications.title: Dissociating Resting-State Networks of Pedohebephilic Preference and Child Sexual Offending Using Network-Based Prediction
publications.abstract: ABSTRACT Pedohebephilia (P+), the sexual preference for prepubescent and early pubertal minors, regularly causes distress in those affected. While associated with child sexual offending (CSO), P+ is not a prerequisite for CSO. Limited neuroimaging studies have identified alterations associated with P+, while these may primarily reflect offending history. The correlates of P+ independent of CSO therefore remain unclear. We examined this distinction using intrinsic functional networks within a multivariate predictive framework. Using resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) and network-based prediction (NBS-Predict), we performed pairwise classifications among non-offending pedohebephilic men (P+CSO-, n =35), pedohebephilic men with CSO (P+CSO+, n =38), and non-pedohebephilic controls without CSO (P-CSO-, n =63). Classification-relevant subnetwork nodal strength was associated post hoc with trait impulsivity within P+ groups. P+CSO- were significantly distinguished from P-CSO- (balanced accuracy [BAC]=.621, p FDR =.041), and showed reductions between default-mode hubs and temporoparietal somatomotor and ventral attention regions. P+CSO+ were also significantly distinguished from P+CSO- (BAC=.645, p FDR =.032) and yielded a smaller subnetwork centered on the substantia nigra. Against P-CSO-, P+CSO+ showed widespread reductions, particularly across subcortical, default mode, visual, limbic, and somatomotor regions (BAC=.640, p FDR =.032). Right precentral gyrus nodal strength correlated with impulsivity in P+CSO+ only ( r = .57, p FDR =.024). Whole-brain rsFC contains information, distinguishing pedohebephilic preference in the absence of known CSO, while P+CSO+ show additional, more widespread network alterations involving systems implicated in action selection and behavioral regulation. These findings open new avenues for integrating pedohebephilia into broader neurobiological research frameworks.

publications.title: Predicting alcohol consumption from resting-state functional connectivity: Feature relevance and the potential of meta-matching
publications.abstract: Abstract Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is among the most prevalent mental disorders. Associations between resting-state fMRI functional connectivity (FC) and AUD have been reported but rarely replicated. In this preregistered study, we investigated the extent to which FC predicts alcohol consumption, as measured by the AUDIT-C score, in a large sample of non–treatment-seeking alcohol consumers (N = 739), including 528 participants with varying degrees of AUD severity. To optimize performance, we compared kernel ridge regression (KRR) trained directly on this sample with transfer-learning models based on multilayer meta-matching embeddings, from which we derived data-driven relevance maps at the connection, region, and network levels. We tested split-half reliability, reproducibility across cohorts, and outcome specificity of the relevance maps. Both models predicted AUDIT-C scores moderately but significantly ( r ≈ 0.15). Meta-matching did not outperform KRR in prediction. Relevance maps showed limited split-half reliability, consistent with the modest predictive performance, but reproduced moderately well across two independent cohorts. These maps indicate reduced connectivity among limbic regions, the anterior middle temporal gyrus, the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, and dorsal attention network regions. In contrast, hypothesized hyperconnectivity patterns involving the striatum, anterior cingulate cortex, and precuneus were less reliable and mostly non-significant. Overall, our findings suggest that resting-state FC contains reproducible but weak signals related to alcohol consumption. Transfer learning improved relevance-map reliability but not prediction performance and reduced outcome specificity. These results support the utility of interpretable machine learning for identifying connectivity patterns related to drinking behavior, while also highlighting current limitations in its predictive power.

publications.title: Differential resting-state functional connectivity of anterior and posterior cerebellar divisions with canonical networks in PTSD
publications.abstract: Background Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a complex psychiatric condition that may develop following exposure to a singular or series of traumatic events producing disruptions in cognitive and affective processes. Although the cerebellum is traditionally linked to voluntary movement coordination and balance, recent work highlights posterior cerebellar regions are involved in affective and cognitive functions. Our goal was to investigate functional connectivity between the cerebellum and canonical cortical resting-state networks in PTSD, with a particular focus on the posterior cerebellum based on previously reported structural changes associated with PTSD on the posterior cerebellum. Methods A total of 313 participants ( M age = 35, 218 females) were comprised of two groups; 119 PTSD patients and 194 healthy controls from eight study sites within the ENIGMA-PTSD working group. The cerebellum was segmented using ACAPULCO into posterior and anterior divisions. Resting-state fMRI preprocessed with HALFpipe was used to assess the functional connectivity of the anterior and posterior divisions of the cerebellum with major canonical cortical networks. Results Compared to the non-PTSD control group, the PTSD group had greater connectivity of the posterior cerebellum with somatomotor (t=4.32, p=0.040) and default mode (t=4.41, p=0.040) networks. Correspondingly, PTSD symptom severity was linked to greater connectivity differentially affecting the posterior relative to the anterior cerebellum with major cortical networks. PTSD symptom severity was positively associated with greater posterior cerebellum connectivity with the default mode (t=4.32, p fdr =0.020), somatomotor (t=3.57, p fdr =0.040), limbic (t=3.74, p fdr =0.036), salience (t=3.61, p fdr =0.040) and central executive network (t=3.59, p fdr =0.040). Conclusion PTSD symptom severity is associated with altered connectivity of the posterior cerebellum with default mode, salience and central executive networks. Cortical connections with the posterior cerebellum, an important socioemotional hub, are involved in PTSD pathology.

publications.title: Does neural variability during acute psychosocial stress capture stress-related brain–body associations?
publications.abstract: Acute psychosocial stress and brain-body coupling Acute psychosocial stress elicits coordinated neural, endocrine, cardiovascular, affective, and behavioral responses that enable adaptation to changing environmental demands (De Kloet et al., 2005; Lupien et al., 2009). These responses unfold across different timescales and show substantial inter-individual variability. At the peripheral level, the autonomic nervous system responds rapidly through sympathetic activation, whereas activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenocortical (HPA) axis results in the delayed release of cortisol (De Kloet et al., 2005; Jankord & Herman, 2008). At the neural level, psychosocial stress engages distributed limbic, salience-processing, default-mode, and executive-control regions involved in threat detection, self-referential processing, cognitive control, and regulation of physiological arousal (Hermans et al., 2014; Menon, 2011; Van Oort et al., 2017). The ScanSTRESS paradigm provides an established functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI)- compatible framework for investigating these coordinated stress responses (see Figure 1). During alternating stress and control blocks, participants perform demanding mental arithmetic and mental rotation tasks under time pressure, social evaluation, and negative feedback (Streit et al., 2014). ScanSTRESS reliably induces neural, endocrine, cardiovascular, affective, and behavioral stress responses (Berretz et al., 2021; Henze et al., 2025; Noack et al., 2019). Our recent harmonized mega-analysis of multi-site ScanSTRESS data demonstrated that conventional task-based blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) responses are systematically associated with different components of the acute stress response (Henze et al., 2025). Cortisol responses were associated with activation in salience- and default-mode-related regions, heart rate with activity in default-mode regions, negative affect with salience- and default-mode activity, and task performance with default-mode and central-executive regions. Several of these brain-body associations additionally differed between male and female participants. Thus, mean task-related BOLD responses capture meaningful inter-individual variation in endocrine, cardiovascular, affective, and behavioral stress reactivity. Importantly, neural stress responses also change over the course of stress exposure. Previous ScanSTRESS studies identified an exposure-time effect characterized by decreasing neural activation from the first to the second ScanSTRESS run (Henze et al., 2020, 2025). Altered exposure-time effects have also been observed in clinical populations, including individuals with burnout symptoms during ScanSTRESS (Bärtl et al., 2024) and patients with major depressive disorder during the Montreal Imaging Stress Task (MIST, (Dong et al., 2022). Notably, such temporal alterations can emerge even in the absence of pronounced differences in overall mean neural stress responses. These findings suggest that temporal characteristics of neural stress processing may contain meaningful information beyond average activation levels and further motivate the investigation of measures that capture dynamic aspects of the BOLD signal. Beyond mean BOLD: Neural variability Task-based fMRI studies conventionally quantify neural responses as average BOLD signal differences between experimental conditions. Although this meanBOLD approach provides information about the overall magnitude and direction of neural responses, it necessarily collapses fluctuations occurring within a condition into a single average value. This may be particularly limiting for acute psychosocial stress, during which participants continuously adapt to changing cognitive demands, social-evaluative threat, negative feedback, and physiological arousal (Dickerson & Kemeny, 2004). Beyond this conceptual limitation, meanBOLD measures also show limited test-retest reliability in many task-based fMRI contexts, with average intraclass correlations often below .40 (Elliott et al., 2020; Tsikonofilos et al., 2025). Together, these conceptual and psychometric limitations motivate the investigation of complementary neural measures that may better capture dynamic aspects of brain function and individual differences in stress processing. Neural variability (NV) provides a complementary way of characterizing such temporal fluctuations. It can be quantified as the standard deviation of the BOLD signal over time (BOLD-SD) and thereby captures moment-to-moment variation in neural activity rather than its average level. BOLD variability, historically often regarded primarily as noise, has increasingly been associated with meaningful aspects of neural functioning, including cognitive performance, flexible transitions between brain states, and adaptation to changing task demands (Garrett et al., 2011; Uddin, 2020; Waschke et al., 2021). Importantly, BOLD-SD appears to capture information that is not redundant with conventional meanBOLD. Direct comparisons have demonstrated largely non-overlapping spatial patterns of BOLD-SD and meanBOLD, and BOLD-SD has shown substantial predictive utility for individual differences in cognitive and clinical characteristics (Garrett et al., 2010, 2011; Månsson et al., 2022; Schneider et al., 2024; Wehrheim et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2018). These findings raise the possibility that BOLD-SD may capture dynamic aspects of neural stress processing that remain hidden when neural responses are summarized by their average magnitude alone. Research gap Despite growing evidence that NV reflects meaningful individual differences in brain function, BOLD-SD has not yet been systematically examined during acute psychosocial stress induction. It therefore remains unknown whether stress-related neural variability is associated with the endocrine, cardiovascular, affective, and behavioral components of an acute psychosocial stress response and whether it provides information beyond conventional meanBOLD measures. The present study builds directly on the ScanSTRESS mega-analysis of Henze et al. (2025). Using the same harmonized multi-site framework, we will examine whether stress-related BOLD-SD is associated with cortisol responses, heart rate, negative affect, and task performance. Given previous evidence that neural stress responses and their associations with peripheral and affective stress-response measures differ between male and female participants (Henze et al., 2025), we will additionally investigate sex differences in stress-related BOLD-SD and in its associations with these stress-response measures.
topics: Heart Rate Variability and Autonomic Control

publications.title: Immune-related gene expression links anxiety, depression, and pain outcomes in adolescence
publications.abstract: BACKGROUND: Chronic pain and internalising disorders such as anxiety and depression frequently co-occur during adolescence. Although prospective associations between internalising symptoms and later pain have been reported previously, the biological mechanisms underlying individual differences in this relationship remain poorly understood. Immune- and oxidative stress-related pathways, including the NRF2 gene, may contribute to such variability. This study investigated whether polymorphisms in the NRF2 gene (rs6721961 and rs35652124) are related to the association between anxiety and depression symptoms at age 14-15 and pain complaints two years later at age 16-17. METHODS: Data were drawn from the IMAGEN longitudinal study (N = 724). Anxiety and depression symptoms were assessed using the Development and Well-Being Assessment (DAWBA), and pain complaints were measured via the Children's Somatization Inventory (CSI). Genotyping was conducted for NRF2 SNPs rs6721961 and rs35652124. Regression analyses tested main effects, followed by genotype-stratified analyses. RESULTS: Consistent with previous literature, higher levels of anxiety and depression at age 14-15 predicted increased pain complaints at age 16-17. Carriers of the TG/TT genotype of rs6721961 had significantly lower anxiety scores and reported fewer pain complaints compared to those carrying the GG genotype of rs6721961. Notably, the association between anxiety and later pain was significant only among individuals with the GG genotype. CONCLUSION: While replicating established associations between adolescent early internalising symptoms and later pain, this study suggests that genetic variation in NRF2 is related to the anxiety-pain association. Specifically, rs6721961 is associated with differences in susceptibility to pain among adolescents with elevated anxiety symptoms.
topics: Child and Adolescent Psychosocial and Emotional Development

name: Hermann Kolanoski
topics: Particle physics theoretical and experimental studies

publications.title: IceCube neutrino point-source searches in the direction of the KM3NeT ultra-high-energy event
publications.abstract: While still under construction, the KM3NeT Astroparticle Research with Cosmics in the Abyss (ARCA) detector recorded a $\sim$200 PeV neutrino on February 13th, 2023. This event is the highest-energy neutrino reported. IceCube, a cubic kilometer neutrino detector located at the geographic South Pole, has previously detected neutrinos up to approximately 10 PeV. We search for high-energy neutrinos from the location of the KM3NeT event using 15 years of IceCube data and considering three temporal hypotheses: steady or flaring in time coincidence, or at an arbitrary time. We find no evidence for neutrino emission for any of the studies performed. Correspondingly, we set upper limits on the neutrino flux from a point source in the direction of KM3-230213A. We compare these limits to KM3NeT's estimated flux and show that an astrophysical explanation of this event is strongly constrained for a variety of spectral assumptions for a steady or transient point source with the flux inferred from the single KM3NeT ultra-high-energy event assuming a spectral index of 2.0.

publications.title: Time-Integrated Searches for Sub-TeV Neutrino Sources with IceCube-DeepCore
publications.abstract: We have developed techniques for a competitive sub-TeV time-integrated neutrino search and applied it to 11.1 years of IceCube-DeepCore data. The DeepCore subarray lowers the sensitivity of IceCube down to sub-TeV energies and is especially interesting for objects with soft spectra. Three studies were performed: a search for neutrino emission from AGN exhibiting high intrinsic X-ray flux, including NGC 1068, as identified by SWIFT/BAT; a search for neutrino emission from Galactic objects identified by Fermi-LAT as exhibiting a spectral shape consistent with neutral pion decay; and an all-sky search for neutrino point sources. Objects for this study were selected given their prospects for sub-TeV neutrino emission. No evidence for sub-TeV neutrino emission is found in any of the searches performed. Finally, for each catalog of objects, we use a statistical combination of the p-values via a binomial test to search for aggregated neutrino emission from a subset of the objects. Neither of the binomial tests yields significant results. For NGC 1068, assuming a power law spectrum with index 3.4, the 90% confidence level upper limit on per-flavor neutrino emission in the 30--400 GeV range is $Φ_{ν+\barν}|_{\mathrm{1 TeV}} < 9.5 \times 10^{-11}$ TeV$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, a factor of two higher than the extrapolation of IceCube's measurement at higher energies. We additionally provide neutrino flux upper limits for a variety of spectra.

publications.title: WavePID: low-energy flavor identification using single-PMT time series in IceCube
publications.abstract: Abstract The IceCube Neutrino Observatory, a cubic-kilometer detector at the South Pole, identifies neutrino flavor through event morphology. Sparse photon detection makes this classification particularly challenging in the 5–100 GeV regime, the energy range relevant for oscillation measurements and searches for physics beyond the Standard Model. We introduce WavePID , a template-based log-likelihood-ratio classifier that exploits nanosecond-scale timing on individual detector modules through three observables: the distance to the reconstructed vertex, the early-charge fraction, and the module-to-module time difference. Evaluated on a cascade-enriched sample selected by a state-of-the-art graph neural network, WavePID improves both cascade purity and classification performance over the neural network alone. This demonstrates that per-module pulse timing carries flavor-identification information complementary to morphology-based classifiers, opening a new physics-motivated observable for low-energy neutrino reconstruction. Geant4 simulations associate this signal with differences in Cherenkov emission geometry between muon tracks and electromagnetic showers. These results motivate exploiting nanosecond-scale pulse timing in future low-energy classifiers and in detector designs with improved per-module timing in next-generation neutrino telescopes.

publications.title: Search for Neutrinos from Tidal Disruption Events with IceCube
publications.abstract: Tidal disruption events (TDEs) are theorized to produce high-energy neutrinos through photohadronic interactions between accelerated protons and multi-wavelength photons in the accretion disk and outflows. Detecting these neutrinos would provide insight into the dynamics of TDEs. Taking advantage of the recent increase in observed TDEs from wide field-of-view telescopes, we conduct a dedicated search for neutrinos coincident in optical/UV and X-ray wavelengths. We searched for neutrino emission from 89 TDEs selected based on X-ray and optical/UV observations using time-dependent likelihood analysis methods in two parts. First, we searched for emission from individual sources, where we fit the time window of expected neutrino emission. Second, we performed a study of jetted and non-jetted TDE subpopulations using a stacking search with a fixed one year time window. No significant neutrino excess was observed in either search. We set upper limits to the contribution of jetted and non-jetted TDEs detected in optical/UV and X-ray wavelengths to the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux assuming TDEs are standard candles.

publications.title: Searching for Extra Dimensions and Copies of the Standard Model with IceCube
publications.abstract: The hierarchy problem remains an open question in particle physics. A number of theories that address this problem lower the fundamental scale of gravity, resulting in observable consequences in the neutrino sector. In this work, we place constraints on low-scale gravity scenarios using high-energy neutrinos observed with the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. The analysis is based on 10.7 years of upward-going muon neutrino data in the energy range from 0.5 to 100 TeV. In this energy range, the theories predict characteristic spectral distortions arising from matter effects when neutrinos propagate through Earth. In the context of large extra dimension models, we constrain the compactification radius of the largest extra dimension to $R \lesssim 0.17\,μ\mathrm{m}$ at $90\%$ confidence level for both normal and inverted neutrino mass ordering. For scenarios with multiple Standard Model copies, we obtain lower limits of up to $N \gtrsim \mathcal{O}(400)$, depending on the value of the lightest neutrino mass. In parts of the parameter space, these results constitute the strongest constraints in the literature to our knowledge, while in other regions they probe previously unexplored parameter space.
topics: Particle physics theoretical and experimental studies

publications.title: Net zero weakens the land carbon sink but land-based mitigation compensates
publications.abstract: Abstract Land ecosystems absorb about a fifth of human CO₂ emissions, mostly because rising CO₂ stimulates plant growth. National greenhouse gas inventories count this land carbon sink on managed land as anthropogenic. Mitigation pathways count only the land-use flux, the emissions and removals from land use. To match inventories, external sink estimates are added to pathways afterwards. Here we compute both components inside the integrated assessment framework LPJmL-MAgPIE-REMIND for six CMIP7 scenarios, with the land’s response to climate change and CO₂ included. In scenarios reaching net-zero CO₂ around mid-century, atmospheric CO₂ declines and the sink on managed land weakens. We show that the sink weakens later than in Grassi et al. and does not become a source, unlike in Gidden et al. Land-based mitigation, such as afforestation, turns the land-use flux from a net emission today into net removals that by 2100 more than compensate for the weaker sink. Inventories count the sum of the sink and the land-use flux. In our net-zero scenarios, this sum peaks in 2050–2070, then loses about 25% by 2100. With our sink counted, net-zero CO₂ comes 2 to 7 years earlier than with the land-use flux alone, and at most 3 with either external estimate.

publications.title: Precision justice in climate adaptation: Diagnosing asymmetric climate risk to target intersectional vulnerability – A Kenyan study with global implications
Land-use, emissions, and sustainability futures across ScenarioMIP-CMIP7: a multi-model assessment
publications.abstract: Managing the global land system requires balancing food, energy, and material production with climate change mitigation and ecosystem conservation, while the agriculture, forestry, and other land use (AFOLU) sector accounts forroughly 20% of anthropogenic greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Here we provide the first multi-model assessment of land-use and AFOLU GHG futures for the new CMIP7 scenario generation, which spans scenarios of climate-policy failure to deep sustainability transformation, enriching the portfolio of assessed land-based mitigation options and addingexplicit demand-side and overshoot pathways. Using seven structurally diverse integrated assessment models (IAMs)across seven marker scenarios and a range of non-marker scenarios of ScenarioMIP-CMIP7, four findings emerge.Weak-policy pathways (H-SSP3, M-SSP2) fail simultaneously on climate change mitigation, food security, and biodiversity loss prevention, with continued agricultural expansion, deforestation, and high AFOLU emissions. Ambitious mitigation turns the land sector into a strong carbon sink by 2100, but the route matters: supply-side bioenergy and BECCS (bioenergy with carbon capture and storage; L-SSP2) deliver worse outcomes than integrated demand-side transformation (VL-SSP1) for biodiversity, agricultural non-CO₂ emissions, nitrogen pollution, and food security, a two-marker contrast rather than an ensemble result; delayed action (LN-SSP2, ML-SSP2, HL-SSP5) aggravates these challenges. Demand-side transformation (dietary shifts, food-waste reduction) and systemic supply-side productivity gains enable sustainable mitigation, consistent with the eradication of hunger assumed in VL-SSP1. Mitigation also reshapes land unevenly across regions (reforestation in Latin America, bioenergy feedstock production in Asia, and cropland expansion in Middle East & Africa under delayed action) concentrating the mitigation burden where governance and food security are often weakest, making the equity of these transitions decisive. By developing the CMIP7 markerscenarios across a structurally diverse model ensemble, this study provides a solid land-sector foundation for next sustainability assessments such as the IPCC AR7 and IPBES assessment cycles.

publications.title: Navigating global health futures under the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways
publications.abstract: The Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) provide valuable insights to understand how future socioeconomic changes could alter the magnitude and pattern of climate-related risks across sectors, which might facilitate or hinder adaptation and mitigation responses. Many sectors have created SSP narrative extensions to specify insights for their domains. In this Viewpoint, we created health narrative extensions for the SSPs, considering socioeconomic and demographic drivers and population health and health-system drivers. The projected health-relevant trajectories diverge substantially over the course of the 21st century. The SSP3 and SSP4 narratives detail changes that could contribute considerable risks to health, whereas the SSP1 and SSP5 narratives highlight the role of effective governance and adequate resourcing in reducing climate-sensitive population health outcomes and health-system drivers. Given that climate forcing is considered exogenous to these narrative extensions, SSP5's favourable health driver paths do not account for the potential adverse impacts of this high-emissions pathway. The narratives elaborate population health drivers that can improve the policy relevance of population health and health-system risk projections associated with climate change across a range of possible pathways, and link these drivers with relevant cross-sectoral issues (eg, water and energy). Further research is required to quantify key drivers of population health and health-system risks at global to local scales.

publications.title: What will it take? Voices on just and feasible food systems

name: Igor M. Sokolov
topics: Complex Systems and Time Series Analysis

publications.title: The Inverse Mean First-Passage Time Problem
publications.abstract: We consider the mean first-passage time $τ(x)$ for an overdamped particle in a one-dimensional potential landscape, and address the problem inverse to the textbook one: Given $τ(x)$ as a function of starting distance, we look for a potential that realizes it. We derive the conditions on $τ(x)$ under which such a potential exists. We show that while the power-law dependences $τ(x)\sim x^α$ with $α\leq 2$ may be realized by monotonic potentials, any realizable $τ(x)$ with superquadratic growth requires potential wells arbitrarily far from the target; $α= 2$ separates sliding from trapping-dominated motion regimes.

publications.title: Formal Fluctuation-Response Relations for Non-Stationary Systems: The Dynamic Conjugate Variable
publications.abstract: Fluctuation-response relations (FRRs) connect the linear response of a system to an external perturbation with properties of spontaneous fluctuations in the unperturbed system. We provide a simple derivation of FRRs for non-stationary dynamics following an almost standard way based on introducing a variable conjugated to perturbation (a dynamic conjugate). The derivation relies solely on the Markovianity of the underlying dynamics, with the only additional assumption that the transition PDF of the process is differentiable with respect to the strength of a constant, time- independent perturbation. The structure of this conjugate variable is however unusual: it is a two-time one, and reduces to a usual single-time conjugate in stationary situations. We show how several known results follow from this approach.
topics: Complex Systems and Time Series Analysis

publications.title: Genuine and Spurious (Non-)Ergodicity in Single Particle Tracking
publications.abstract: In single-particle tracking experiments measuring anomalous diffusion dynamics, understanding ergodicity is crucial, as it ensures that the time average of an observable matches the ensemble average—and can thus be fitted with known ensemble-averaged observables. A commonly used criterion for assessing the ergodicity of a stochastic process is based on the comparison of the mean-squared displacement (MSD) with the time-averaged MSD (TAMSD). This approach has been widely applied and proves effective in cases of weak ergodicity breaking across various systems in both theoretical and experimental studies. However, there is relatively little discussion regarding the theoretical justification and limitations of this definition. Here, we demonstrate that this widely accepted criterion to some extent contradicts the classical definition of ergodicity as well as physical intuition, leading to spurious (non-)ergodicity results when applied to several well-known stochastic models. To address this limitation, we propose using the mean-squared increment (MSI) instead of the MSD for comparison of ensemble- and time-averaged observables. For processes with stationary increments, the results for MSI and MSD coincide. However, if the increments of the process reach stationarity at long times only, they differ, and the MSI-TAMSD comparison still provides the test for ergodicity. Several well-established examples demonstrate, through both trajectory simulations and theoretical analysis, that our MSI-TAMSD criterion provides a more accurate characterization of the genuine (non-)ergodicity of systems where the MSD-TAMSD method fails. Additionally, for systems exhibiting “ultraweak” ergodicity breaking, the MSI can reveal the asymptotic stationarity and ergodic nature of the process’s increments. Our findings emphasize the important role of the MSI observable for SPT experiments and anomalous diffusion studies.

publications.title: Fluctuation-response relation for a nonequilibrium system with resolved Markovian embedding
publications.abstract: Fluctuation-response relations must be modified to describe nonequilibrium systems with non-Markovian dynamics. Here, we experimentally demonstrate that such relation is quantitatively recovered when the appropriate Markovian embedding of the dynamics is explicitly resolved. Using a colloidal particle optically trapped in a harmonic potential and driven out of equilibrium by a controlled colored noise, we study the response to a perturbation of the stiffness of the confining potential. While the reduced dynamics violates equilibrium fluctuation-response relations, we show that the dynamical response to the stiffness perturbation is fully determined by steady-state correlations involving the exact conjugate observable in the Markovian embedding.

publications.title: Coherent effects in quantum transport models and their classical counterparts
publications.abstract: We analyze the transport properties of quasiparticles locally excited at an initial time moment in several exactly solvable quantum models. It is revealed that, in the investigated quantum systems, the time-dependent probability distribution function (PDF) exhibits behavior similar to that of classical continuous-time random walk (CTRW) models, such as Lévy walks or diffusing diffusivity.

name: J. Kretzschmar
topics: Particle physics theoretical and experimental studies

publications.title: Measurement of isolated photon plus two-jet correlations in Pb+Pb and pp collisions at 5.02 TeV with ATLAS
publications.abstract: This paper presents a measurement of photon plus two-jet events in pp and Pb+Pb collisions, i.e. events in which the transverse momentum of a single photon is balanced by two distinct jets. The measurement was performed using pp data taken in 2017 with an integrated luminosity 260 pb − 1 , and Pb+Pb data taken in 2018 with an integrated luminosity 1.72 nb − 1 , both at s NN =5.02 TeV, as recorded by the ATLAS detector. Events with photons in the transverse momentum range 90–180 GeV and at least two anti- k t R = 0.2 jets with a p T > 30 GeV are selected, and three observables are measured: x JJ γ , A JJ γ , and Δ R JJ . These observables characterise the overall energy loss of the multiparton system from medium interactions (x JJ γ ), the relative energy loss between the two colour-charge carriers (A JJ γ ), and medium-induced modifications to their opening angle (Δ R JJ ). The observables are corrected for uncorrelated combinatoric background contributions using a novel multijet mixing technique, for photon purity, and for detector resolution effects via iterative unfolding. Final results are presented per photon, and the ratio ( I AA ) is taken between measurements in Pb+Pb and pp collisions, for Pb+Pb centrality intervals of 30–80%, 10–30%, and 0–10%. Significant suppression of per photon two-jet yields in all three observables, I AA < 1, is observed as a result of parton-medium interactions. The experimental measurements are compared to three different jet quenching models: Jewel , Jetscape , and Lbt .
topics: Particle physics theoretical and experimental studies

publications.title: Search for $$ t\overline{t} $$ resonances in final states with exactly one or two leptons using 140 fb−1 of pp collision data at $$ \sqrt{s}=13 $$ TeV with the ATLAS experiment
publications.abstract: A bstract A search for heavy spin-1 and spin-2 resonances decaying into a top-antitop-quark pair has been performed with 140 fb − 1 of proton-proton collision data collected by the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider at a centre-of-mass energy of $$ \sqrt{s}=13 $$ s = 13 TeV. Final states with either exactly one electron or muon, or exactly two leptons ( ee , μμ or eμ ), large missing transverse momentum, and two jets, at least one of which must be identified as likely containing a b -hadron decay, are considered. The search targets resonances with both narrow and broad widths relative to the detector resolution, and with masses in the range of 0.4–5.0 TeV. No significant deviation from the Standard Model prediction is observed. Exclusion limits are set on the production cross-section times branching ratio for hypothetical Z′ bosons, Kaluza-Klein gravitons, and Kaluza-Klein gluons that decay into top-quark pairs.
topics: Particle physics theoretical and experimental studies

publications.title: Search for soft unclustered energy patterns containing muons in the final state in pp collisions at $$ \sqrt{s}=13 $$ TeV with the ATLAS detector
publications.abstract: A bstract Soft unclustered energy patterns (SUEPs) refer to high-multiplicity, isotropic distributions of low-momentum particles that could arise in strongly-coupled hidden sector theories. A search for SUEPs whose decay products contain muons in the final state is presented using 140 fb − 1 of proton–proton collision data at $$ \sqrt{s}=13 $$ s = 13 TeV collected by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider during 2015–2018. The analysis targets SUEP signatures via gluon–gluon fusion production of a scalar mediator in Hidden Valley scenarios. No significant excess over the Standard Model expectation is observed. Exclusion limits are set on the product of the mediator production cross section and the branching fraction for its decay into a SUEP, down to 0.05 fb for a mediator mass of m S = 750 GeV, 0.4 fb for m S = 400 GeV, and 70 fb for m S = 125 GeV; the last value, when identifying the mediator with the Standard Model Higgs boson, translates to an upper limit on the branching fraction of around 0.2%.
topics: Particle physics theoretical and experimental studies

publications.title: Observation of pair production of longitudinally polarized Z bosons in four-lepton final state with the ATLAS detector
publications.abstract: The production of two longitudinally polarized bosons is measured using proton–proton collision data recorded by the ATLAS experiment at a center-of-mass energy √ = 13.6 TeV and with an integrated luminosity of 164 fb−1. The candidate events are reconstructed using two same-flavor opposite-charge electron or muon pairs. The polarization fractions of the boson pair are measured inclusively in the fiducial phase space and also in two regions of the four-lepton invariant mass, and the results are consistent with the Standard Model predictions. After a statistical combination with a previous measurement at √ = 13 TeV, the first observation of the production of two simultaneously longitudinally polarized bosons is obtained, with observed and expected significances of 6.5 and 5.6 standard deviations, respectively.

publications.title: Search for a leptoquark in events with a hadronically decaying τ-lepton and missing transverse momentum using pp collisions at s=13TeV with the ATLAS detector
publications.abstract: A search for leptoquark signals is performed in final states with a hadronically decaying τ -lepton and missing transverse momentum, using data from proton–proton collisions at a centre-of-mass energy of s = 13 TeV recorded by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider during Run 2 (2015–18), corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 140 fb − 1 . The analysis is designed to probe both resonant production and non-resonant t -channel exchange of the leptoquark, covering a wide range of coupling scenarios. No excess above the Standard Model background prediction is observed. Limits are set on the couplings in the benchmark U 1 vector-leptoquark model at 95% confidence level for masses between 1.5 TeV and 3.0 TeV.

publications.title: Regional Patterns in the Prevalence of Patient‐Reported Urticaria Aggravating Factors: A Multinational Mobile Health Study
publications.abstract: BACKGROUND: In chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU), exacerbations are often associated with aggravating factors. However, the prevalence of patients having aggravating factors has been insufficiently studied. This mHealth study aimed to (i) estimate the prevalence of patient-reported perceived aggravating factors for CSU across 10 countries, and (ii) identify factors associated with such triggers. METHODS: We performed a cross-sectional analysis of data from users of the CRUSE mobile application. The study included patients aged 15-74 years with self-reported CSU. We assessed the frequency of reporting at least one of the following perceived aggravating factors: stress, food, exercise, low or high temperature, rubbing of the skin, infection, and medication. To correct for sample biases in age and sex distribution, we employed Multilevel Regression with Poststratification (MRP) models. In addition, we built logistic regression models to identify factors associated with perceived aggravating factor reporting. RESULTS: Of the 12,243 included participants, 62.1% reported at least one perceived aggravating factor. Stress (31.1%) and rubbing of the skin (23.1%) were the most common. After MRP, the frequency of reporting at least one perceived aggravating factor ranged between 39.6% (Japan) and 83.7% (Brazil). The reporting frequency was lower in Asian than in Western countries. Female sex was independently associated with higher odds of reporting most perceived aggravating factors, except exercise and food. Younger age and lower disease control were associated with higher aggravating factor reporting. CONCLUSIONS: Patient-reported perceived aggravating factors varied substantially across countries. Female sex, younger age, and poorer disease control were associated with increased reporting. Cross-country differences may reflect biological, healthcare-related, cultural, and psychosocial influences.

publications.title: Onset of Action of Azelastine 0.15% Versus Olopatadine/Mometasone for Allergen‐Induced Rhinitis: An EEU Crossover Study
publications.abstract: BACKGROUND: The aim of this study was to compare the onset of action (primary), and overall efficacy (secondary) of azelastine nasal spray 0.15% (AZE 0.15%) with mometasone/olopatadine combination therapy (OloMom) in subjects with allergen-induced rhinitis under controlled allergen exposure conditions in an Environmental Exposure Unit (EEU). METHOD: This was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, three-period Williams cross-over study. Participants were randomized to receive AZE 0.15%, OloMom, or placebo. Efficacy was assessed during two pollen challenge sections in an EEC, after a single dose and after 3.5 days of treatment. Following a minimum 14-day washout period, subjects received alternate treatment and repeated study procedures until all three interventions were evaluated. The primary endpoint was time to onset of action based on change from baseline in Total Nasal Symptom Score (TNSS). Secondary assessments included total and individual nasal and ocular symptoms and overall efficacy after 3.5 days of treatment. RESULTS: Eighty-four subjects completed the study (mean age 41.5 years; balanced sex distribution), all with confirmed ragweed sensitivity. All treatments reduced TNSS post-dose, with most effective and fastest relief from AZE 0.15%, onset at 15 minutes, sensitivity analyses supported onset at 10 minutes, and greater early nasal, ocular, and total symptom relief compared to OloMom and placebo. CONCLUSION: AZE 0.15% delivered rapid and clinically significant relief of AR, demonstrating greater early symptoms improvement compared with OloMom. Overall efficacy was comparable between treatments, supporting AZE 0.15% as an effective, steroid-free alternative for rapid symptom control in patients with pollen allergies.

publications.title: Natural Diversity of Grass Pollen in Europe—An EAACI Perspective
publications.abstract: Grass pollen, the most clinically relevant outdoor aeroallergen in Europe and worldwide, presents a complex challenge due to the diverse nature of its subspecies. This diversity complicates the interpretation of their contribution to the overall pollen burden during the grass pollen season and the selection of the appropriate allergen immunotherapy. Almost all species of the Pooideae subfamily share important major allergens, namely the allergens of Group 1 and 5, leading to a high level of cross-reactivity at the IgE level. However, the presence of a multitude of additional minor allergens and species-specific epitopes adds to the complexity. Timothy (Phleum pratense), previously considered the most relevant allergen source among grass species, is found during the late-blooming grass pollen season, while symptom severity and pollen concentrations already show several peaks during the early-blooming grass and main grass pollen seasons. Current data suggest a limited regional relevance of timothy grass during the natural grass pollen season in southern Europe from both the aerobiology and allergy perspectives. This review aims to discuss the latest evidence supporting a broad-spectrum approach to best reflect natural grass pollen exposure in allergen immunotherapy, presenting a complex but crucial aspect of allergology.

publications.title: Reply to “Underlying assumptions used in a network meta-analysis can alter the conclusions”
Position paper: a coordinated approach to fracture and fall prevention from seven international organizations
publications.abstract: Fragility fractures constitute a major global health burden and often result from falls. However, clinical care for fragility fractures is currently organized separately from fall prevention services leading to gaps in integrated care delivery. This joint position paper from the European Geriatric Medicine Society, the Fragility Fracture Network, the World Falls Prevention Society, the European Society for Clinical and Economic Aspects of Osteoporosis, Osteoarthritis and Musculoskeletal Diseases, the International Osteoporosis Foundation, the European Union of Medical Specialists-Geriatric Medicine Section, and the International Association of Gerontology and Geriatrics-European Region highlights the critical need for integrated falls and fracture prevention, with a focus on evidence-based clinical practice, knowledge dissemination, education, policy strategies, and research. We outline existing guidelines on fall and fracture prevention, with particular emphasis on how fracture risk assessment can be incorporated into fall prevention services and on integrating fall assessment into fracture prevention services. We advocate that future implementation guidelines place greater emphasis on fully integrated models of care. Moreover, training and education programs should be designed to encourage interdisciplinary collaboration among healthcare professionals. Integrated fall and fracture prevention services should be recognized as a public health priority and incorporated into national strategies for healthy aging, supported by adequate, dedicated, and sustainable resources including evidence-based exercise provision. Finally, future research should focus on evaluating the (cost) effectiveness of integrated care models and examining their practical implementation in real-world settings.

publications.title: Multi-predator feeding aggregations in pelagic waters
publications.abstract: Abstract Multi-predator feeding aggregations (MPFAs) are temporary co-occurrences of several species of predators simultaneously exploiting the same prey resource. Pelagic waters are home to the largest and most diverse MPFAs on the planet, however, our knowledge of the mechanisms and functions driving the existence of MPFAs is heavily biased towards terrestrial systems which are characterized by the fight for resource monopolization. By contrast, in pelagic waters, observed interactions between predators rarely involve aggression, presumably because monopolization of large fish schools or zooplankton swarms is difficult or impossible. Additionally, the provision and maintenance of energetically viable prey aggregations may depend on conspecific and heterospecific hunting behaviour. There has been considerable speculation regarding the interactions of predators in pelagic MPFAs, which include sharks, teleost fishes, seabirds, pinnipeds and cetaceans, but these interactions are difficult to observe in situ. Only recently have scientists begun to obtain data on attack and capture rates of predators at pelagic MPFAs which allow insights into whether their interactions are competitive, mutualistic or neutral. In this special edition, we begin by outlining the biomechanical and energetic bases of MPFAs before probing some of the main hypotheses regarding predator interactions at MPFAs. We then address MPFAs from a collective behaviour perspective before ending with some of the broader ecological aspects of MPFAs. Links between MPFAs and socio-economic factors such as marine reserves, sustainable fisheries and eco-tourism practices are discussed throughout the issue's 14 articles. This article is part of the theme issue ‘Multi-predator feeding aggregations in pelagic waters’.

publications.title: How volant seabirds benefit from sub-surface predators during multi-predator feeding aggregations
publications.abstract: Multi-predator feeding aggregations are common in marine ecosystems and frequently involve seabirds. Often labelled opportunistic 'scroungers', volant seabirds derive diverse benefits from the association with sub-surface predators (such as cetaceans, pinnipeds, Teleosts) which can significantly enhance their hunting performance. In this opinion piece, we outline the major mechanisms through which sub-surface predators benefit volant seabirds, based on recent quantitative evidence and hypotheses that warrant further research. The mechanisms we identified are: herding prey to the surface, prey detection (local enhancement), reduction of prey cohesion, access to immobilized prey and the attentional overload of prey. Furthermore, we discuss potential interactions between these mechanisms and mechanism-based predictions which can be tested in the field. We propose that the associations with sub-surface predators are ecologically relevant to the extent that they may influence selection breeding sites. We conclude by discussing methodological advancements that have the possibility to further research in this field and go over open questions they might help to answer in the future. This article is part of the theme issue 'Multi-predator feeding aggregations in the pelagic waters'.

publications.title: The presence of mahi-mahi at multi-predator feeding aggregations modifies striped marlin attack behaviour
publications.abstract: Terrestrial multi-species predator feeding aggregations (MPFAs) are characterized by contest competition, but scramble competition is likely more common at MPFAs in pelagic waters. However, empirical investigations are rare. Aerial video was used to estimate abundances of striped marlin and mahi-mahi alongside their attack and capture rates and spatio-temporal positioning as they competed at prey schools. Mahi-mahi had higher capture efficiencies than marlin, and the presence of marlin did not affect mahi-mahi predatory behaviour. Conversely, the presence of mahi-mahi in smaller abundances may benefit marlin. Marlin attack rates on the school were not affected by mahi-mahi presence, but net capture rates increased, likely explained by a shift in marlin hunting dynamics where marlin increased the proportion of their total captures that were individual fish isolated from the prey school. Estimated abundances of mahi-mahi, however, showed a negative relationship with marlin abundance. As mahi-mahi monopolized the space closest to the prey school, where they made rapid and efficient attacks on the prey school, in large abundances they may interfere with marlin hunting behaviour, causing them to abandon the hunt. The persistence of scramble or contest competition at MPFAs in pelagic waters may therefore be partially modulated by group size. This article is part of the theme issue 'Multi-predator feeding aggregations in pelagic waters'.

publications.title: Ephemeral resources promote adaptive sociality in wild guppies
publications.abstract: Sociality can facilitate the discovery of novel resources, yet it can also entail costs, including increased competition, aggression, sexual harassment and disease transmission. Selection should therefore favour social flexibility as a response to changes in resource conditions, allowing individuals to adjust their social associations optimally. Quantifying these social adjustments and how they allow individuals to benefit in dynamically changing resource environments can provide insight into the adaptive capacity of wild animal populations. We experimentally studied social flexibility in wild guppies Poecilia reticulata by examining their fission–fusion dynamics. Using mixed‐sex sets of individually marked fish, we manipulated recent foraging experience by presenting them with unpredictable, ephemeral food patches or control patches in the wild. Guppies that had been exposed to ephemeral food patches significantly increased their sociality, doubling the proportion of time spent social compared to controls. This shift was driven by both an increase in the probability of starting and a decrease in the probability of ending social contact. Stronger increases in sociality were associated with individuals more often locating ephemeral food patches, mediated by foraging motivation. Importantly, increased sociality was not merely the result of local aggregation, as exposure to ephemeral food patches increased, rather than reduced, spatial activity. Yet, stronger spatial activity did not result in more time spent social. In a second experiment, fish were briefly presented with food patches they could see and smell but not actually consume. Again, fish increased their level of sociality compared to control, indicating that the observed social response was not merely driven by satiation‐related changes in activity budgets. Together, our results highlight the adaptive and dynamic nature of fission–fusion social systems and support the view that wild animals adaptively shape their social environment in response to fluctuations in resource variability.

publications.title: How Accurate Is DFT for Alkanes and Water Adsorbed in Acidic Zeolites?
publications.abstract: Abstract We assess the accuracy of electronic structure methods for modeling the dispersion-dominated adsorption of methane, ethane, and propane, and the adsorption of hydrogen-bonded water in the Brønsted acidic zeolite chabazite (H–CHA) using density functional theory (DFT) with periodic boundary conditions and a hybrid QM:QM (QM = quantum mechanics) approach. In addition to coupled-cluster (CCSD(T)) reference energies, which agree with available experimental values within chemical accuracy limits of ±4 kJ mol–1, we also provide reference adsorption structures obtained with Møller–Plesset perturbation theory (MP2). DFT mostly overestimates binding compared to CCSD(T), with root-mean-square deviations (RMSDs) ranging from 6–29 kJ mol–1 for alkanes and 5–33 kJ mol–1 for water. QM:QM calculations with hybrid functionals as high level can reduce RMSDs from the CCSD(T) reference. With B3LYP+D4 as a high-level method, the QM:QM energies deviate by 7–12 and 11–21 kJ mol–1 for alkanes and water, respectively, depending on the low-level method. With ωB97M-V as high-level method, the RMSDs are 4–10 and 4–15 kJ mol–1, and with MP2, they are 1–3 and 2–8 kJ mol–1, respectively. When ωB97M-V is used as a high-level method or r2SCAN+D4 as a low-level method, predictions for the protonation state of water can be qualitatively wrong. For DFT modeling of periodic systems, when hybrid functionals are not affordable, we recommend revPBE+D3. For QM:QM with hybrid DFT as high-level method, ωB97M-V:revPBE+D3 is the best combination. Only CCSD(T) single points on hybrid MP2 structures reliably deliver chemically accurate adsorption energies and qualitatively correct adsorption structures.

publications.title: Resolving the Structures of AlM2O4+ (M = Fe, Co) through Multireference Methods
publications.abstract: Multicenter transition metal clusters often exhibit a dense manifold of low-lying electronic states arising from the interplay of ligand-field splitting and spin coupling. Together with structural and valence isomerism, these factors make vibrational spectral assignments challenging. The infrared photodissociation (IRPD) spectra of AlM2O4+ (M = Fe, Co) have resisted interpretation because the predicted spectra are sensitive to the isomer and its electronic state. Here we settle the assignment by employing multireference methods in a localized active space framework to identify the low-energy structures and their ground-state electronic configurations, followed by vibrational analysis using Kohn-Sham density functional theory. We show that the experimental IRPD spectra arise from the coexistence of two structural isomers, each in a low-spin ground state. Vibrational spectra calculated for the identified ground states reproduce the experimental IRPD features, whereas those of alternative states do not. This assignment is consistent with reported experimental observations, namely the IRPD spectra, the ion mobility distributions, and the absence of methane reactivity. Analysis of the electronic structure reveals that ligand-field effects dominate over spin coupling in shaping both energetics and vibrational spectra of these clusters. These results show the power of multireference methods capable of treating large active spaces, which are often required for binuclear complexes.

publications.title: Atomistic Model for Water Adsorption in Mg-MOF-74: Quantum Chemical Prediction of Structures and Isotherms
publications.abstract: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide The design of improved metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) for water harvesting requires the reliable prediction of adsorption isotherms, i.e., Gibbs free energies of adsorption, with no other input than the atomic positions. We employ density functional theory (DFT) and show that, in Mg-MOF-74, well-defined adsorption structures exist for water loadings of n = 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 molecules per Mg 2+ ion. The first water molecule attaches to the open metal site, while on adsorption of subsequent molecules, structures with an increasing number of hydrogen bonds per molecule form: dimers ( n = 2), chains in pore direction ( n = 3), and a monolayer on the pore wall ( n = 4). For n = 5, a tube-like stack of water trimers connected to the monolayer fills the pore completely, and all water molecules are 4-fold coordinated. For isotherm predictions, we use a Multisite Langmuir model with Gibbs free energies of −33, −19, −13, −10, and −21 kJ/mol for the steps leading to adsorption states with n = 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 molecules, respectively. The close agreement of the predicted total isotherm with experiment corresponds to an accuracy of ±2 kJ/mol for Gibbs free energies. This is achieved only after adding “high-level” Coupled Cluster corrections (0, 3, 9, 8, and 11 kJ/mol for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively) to the DFT energies. We show that the large variations observed between different experimental isotherms can be explained by sample imperfections or incomplete evacuation of samples before isotherm measurements.

publications.title: Anharmonic Adsorption Free Energies Beyond GGA for Monomer Ethanol in H-ZSM-5
publications.abstract: Zeolites play a pivotal role as catalysts in biomass conversion, and understanding how alcohols interact with these materials is essential for designing next-generation catalysts that reduce dependence on nonrenewable fuels and enable a more sustainable energy landscape. Achieving this understanding requires accurate free-energy calculations. In this study, we present the anharmonic enthalpy, entropy, and vibrational free energy associated with ethanol adsorption on H-ZSM-5, computed at a hybrid DFT level of theory. We critically assess the need to go beyond both GGA functionals and the harmonic approximation to achieve chemically accurate vibrational free energies. The vibrational contributions to the free energy are obtained using a newly implemented strategy that combines the DOS-P method with a QM/QM molecular-dynamics scheme. This approach yields significant improvement in accuracy compared to the commonly used PBE + D2 functional. By combining the anharmonic vibrational free energies computed at the B3LYP + D2 level with electronic energies refined at the CCSD(T) level, we obtain an anharmonic adsorption enthalpy, Δ H, of −101.9 kJ mol –1, the entropic term, − T Δ S, equal to 61.0 kJ mol –1, and a free energy of adsorption, Δ G, of −40.8 kJ mol –1 at 313 K. We performed a critical comparison between these values and the experimental data. Notably, the entropic term agrees well with the experimental value of 62.0 kJ mol –1 . We also examine the significance of anharmonicity, finding a correction of approximately 1 kJ mol –1 for both the vibrational entropy and enthalpy, and about 3.7 kJ mol –1 for the ZPE.

publications.title: Prioritizing Sea-Dumped Munitions for Clearance
publications.abstract: Abstract Prioritizing sea-dumped munition piles for clearance exemplifies a sustainability governance challenge in which spatial decisions must be made amid diverse stakeholder interests and limited scientific information. Here, we present a co-creation process to design a multi-tier index that combines multiple knowledge types within the Analytical Hierarchy Process to enable such decisions. We use the Source-Pathway-Receptor-Consequence model to structure the selection of data sources. We introduce a two-level weighting structure in which stakeholder elicitation reveals preferences, while expert elicitation complements limited scientific information. We apply the process to develop MCA-DuMP, a multi-tier index, to prioritize 39 munition piles in the German Baltic Sea. We identify 10 high-priority piles for clearance, spatial hotspots, and the need to rezone contaminated areas. The index currently supports Germany’s pioneering effort to systematically clear sea-dumped munitions, but can also be applied in other contexts. The co-creation process itself is applicable to spatial prioritization problems in general.

publications.title: Comment on “Flooding Is Not like Filling a Bath” by Sanders et al.
publications.abstract: Abstract In their commentary “Flooding is not like filling a Bath” in Earth's Future ( https://doi.org/10.1029/2024EF005164 ) Sanders and colleagues highlight biases and uncertainties in the application of bathtub modeling for assessing flood risks, specifically for coastal assessments at broad scales (world‐regional to global scales). This is a laudable and timely undertaking. Sanders et al., however, also draw a number of far‐reaching conclusions including a general call to abandon the bathtub model together with a claim that the bathtub model introduces unacceptable levels of uncertainty, and that its broad scale applications have contributed to a “climate hype” exaggerating the impacts of climate change. In our opinion, these conclusions are misleading and don't follow from the author's analysis, because the authors take an overly narrow perspective on flood risk. Addressing this issue, this comment characterizes the system problem of assessing current and future coastal flood risk at broad scales, discusses the roles that bathtub and physics‐based models play in addressing this problem, as well as the implications for communicating and receiving information on future flood risk at broad scale. Three conclusions are drawn. First, there is no one‐size‐fits‐all model for assessing coastal flood hazard at broad scales and the bathtub model and its variants still have a role to play. Second, physics‐based models are computationally too expensive to deliver the multitude of simulations needed for future flood risk and adaptation. Third, future work needs to create a framework to most effectively utilize physics‐based models, emulators of them and bathtub‐based models for broad scale assessments.

publications.title: The economically optimal mix and timing of coastal adaptation in Europe to 2150
publications.abstract: Coastal adaptation to sea level rise involves combining and sequencing adaptation options into adaptation pathways that include adaptation tipping points, which are moments requiring a switch between options, often due to economic limits. While local case studies show costs depend on the economically optimal timing of actions and adaptation tipping points, this remains unexplored on global and continental scales. We present economically optimal adaptation pathways for Europe's coastal floodplains through 2150. For 95% of the coastline requiring adaptation, the optimal timing for initial actions is immediate due to current economic under-adaptation, a condition in which the costs of additional adaptation are outweighed by the reduction in expected flood damages. By 2150, retreat is economically optimal for 22% of the coastline, incurring lower total costs than protection, which is optimal for 9%. Adaptation tipping points are primarily driven by sea level rise and necessitate a switch from accommodation to either protection or retreat, or from retreat to inland protection combined with retreat in the foreland. Their timing depends on climate change, occurring 32 years earlier under higher climate change scenarios compared to lower ones.

publications.title: The Global Economic Case for Immediate and Continuous Coastal Adaptation
publications.abstract: Abstract Despite growing evidence of a global coastal adaptation gap under accelerating sea-level rise, global economic evidence on when and how to close this gap remains scarce. Here, we identify economically optimal adaptation pathways for floodplains worldwide, enabling flexible timing and switching between adaptation options over time. We find that immediate adaptation is economically optimal for 28% of the global coastline, irrespective of the climate change scenario, reflecting that many floodplains are under-adapted today. By 2150, adaptation is economically warranted along 31% of the global coastline, with 20% optimally managed through retreat, 7% through coastal protection, less than 1% through accommodation, and 4% through combined retreat and inland protection. Relative future cost burdens of adaptation investments and flood damages are highest in the Global South, exacerbating inequities embedded in today’s adaptation gap.

publications.title: DIVACoast model results: sea-level rise impacts and adaptation response under different adaptation paradigms
publications.abstract: This dataset contains modelled outputs of the DIVACoast model on flood risk driven by sea-level rise and adaptation response from the ACCREU EU project, structured across three spatial scales: NUTS2/GADM1 (subnational), country and global. The data is organized into two sets: Set 1 - Three Adaptation Paradigms Results modelled under three adaptation strategies: Constant Dike Height (CDH) Constant Flood Protection Standards (CFPS) Optimal Protection (OP) Set 2 - CFPS Sensitivity Runs (_CFPS files): A second set of three CSV files (identifiable by the _CFPS suffix) containing additional sensitivity runs under the Constant Flood Protection Standards paradigm, exploring the effect of doubling and quadrupling CFPS levels by 2100. publications.title: Testing strategy for the identification of thyroid hormone system disrupting chemicals
publications.abstract: Disruption of the thyroid hormone (TH) system during fetal and neonatal life poses a significant risk to human neurodevelopment, yet current regulatory assessments lack sufficiently sensitive and specific endpoints to identify chemicals causing TH system disruption (THSD). The ATHENA project aimed to develop an integrated framework combining in silico, in vitro, and in vivo approaches to improve the identification of substances causing THSD and support their assessment within a regulatory context. This testing strategy emphasizes increased use of the adverse outcome pathways (AOP) framework and read-across approaches to better predict and address adversity. It further provides recommendations for in silico and in vitro test batteries and targeted in vivo investigations to improve identification of chemicals causing THSD. In addition, we propose enhancements to current regulatory practice, including further standardization of test methods, improved integration of human epidemiological and cross-species evidence, and recognition of altered TH concentration in serum and brain in animal studies as predictors of adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes in humans. Collectively, these measures are intended to strengthen chemical hazard assessment and improve protection of human and environmental health through more robust and efficient identification of THSD.

publications.title: Selenoprotein P and type 2 diabetes risk in a large cohort of older German adults
publications.abstract: BACKGROUND: A previous meta-analysis reported an increased type 2 diabetes (T2D) risk at high blood selenium levels but included few prospective cohorts. Here, we assessed the long-term associations of serum SELENOP concentrations and incident T2D in a large cohort. METHODS: Serum SELENOP concentrations were measured at baseline and 5-year follow-up in 6529 participants aged 50-74 years in the German ESTHER study. Multivariable Cox models were performed to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for incident T2D across quintiles (Q) of SELENOP concentrations. RESULTS: During a median follow-up of 11.5 years (interquartile range, 7.1-16.7 years), 1235 participants developed T2D. No statistically significant association between time-dependently modelled SELENOP and T2D risk was observed (HR [95%CI] for Q5 vs. Q1, 1.08 [0.89-1.30]). SELENOP concentrations decreased on average by 0.90 mg/L from baseline to 5-year follow-up. For those 80% of the population, for whom SELENOP decreased by less than 1.83 mg/L, a statistically significant 22% lower T2D risk was observed compared to those 20% with a larger SELENOP decrease (HR [95%CI]: 0.78 [0.62-0.98]). Results were consistent across subgroups defined by sex, age, BMI, smoking status, physical activity level, prediabetes, oxidative stress, inflammatory status, and vitamin D status. CONCLUSIONS: This large prospective cohort study found no increased long-term risk of T2D among older adults residing in Germany with time-dependently modelled SELENOP concentrations. However, although a decrease in SELENOP with ageing is normal, the 20% of the population with the greatest decline in serum SELENOP concentrations showed an increased T2D risk.

Comparative Evaluation of hiPSC-Derived Brain Organoids as Platforms for Assessing Thyroid Hormone System Disrupting Chemicals
publications.abstract: Thyroid hormones (THs) are essential regulators of human brain development, and disrupted TH availability during pregnancy or early life is linked to adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes. Concerns that environmental chemicals interfere with TH signalling have increased the need for human-relevant in vitro systems to identify thyroid hormone system-disrupting chemicals (THSDCs) for risk assessment. Here, we compared two human-induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived brain organoid models for THSDC assessment: (i) human cortical organoids (COs) generated by unguided differentiation, offering higher architectural complexity but lower throughput; and (ii) neural stem cell-derived organoids (NSCOs), designed for scalability with reduced cellular diversity. Both models expressed key TH handling components, including the transporter SLC16A2 (MCT8) and the inactivating enzyme DIO3. Using LC–MS/MS, we show that exogenous T3 is depleted from culture media and metabolized to 3,3′-T2 and 3′-T1 in both models, alongside upregulation of T3-responsive genes (HR, KLF9, DIO3, SEMA3C). Pulse and chronic co-exposures to reference disruptors iopanoic acid (IA, deiodinase inhibitor) and silychristin (SC, MCT8 inhibitor) altered T3 metabolism and modulated T3-responsive transcriptional endpoints. In NSCOs, high-content imaging revealed treatment-associated changes in cell composition, with chronic T3 reducing the SOX2-positive progenitor pool and THSDCs blocking this effect. Together, these findings provide a framework for organoid qualification—linking TH handling, transcriptomic responsiveness, and scalable phenotypic readouts—as a necessary step toward model validation and implementation of brain organoids in THSDC risk assessment pipelines.
