publications.title: PRIMA: Pose Refined Inductive Motion Adapter for Zero Shot Social Bodily Behavior Recognition
publications.abstract: Recognizing fine-grained bodily behaviors, such as self-grooming, postural shifts, and backchanneling, is a useful intermediate step for computational social signal analysis. But the behaviors that matter vary across social contexts, and retraining a model for each new taxonomy is expensive. Vision-language models (VLMs) can adapt to new categories through text prompts, yet they lack sensitivity to body structure and often confuse subtle postural distinctions. We propose PRIMA (Pose Refined Inductive Motion Adapter), a lightweight module that injects a body-structure prior into frozen VLMs using human pose as a training-time supervisory signal, requiring no pose input at inference. PRIMA separates a model-specific projection head from a shared core that encodes transferable body-configuration knowledge; adapting to a new VLM requires retraining only the head. We train PRIMA on a micro-action dataset and evaluate entirely through zero-shot prompting. The adapter improves recognition on its training domain, transfers to additional VLM backbones at different scales with the core frozen, and generalizes to two unseen target datasets from social psychology and daily activity recognition. In a supporting downstream study, the improved behavior predictions also yield higher correlations with human ratings of rapport and dominance in a collaboration context. Within the scope of the tested models and indoor datasets, the results indicate that pose-guided training can produce body-structure priors that generalize across unseen behavior vocabularies and can be partially reused across VLM backbones while preserving RGB-only inference.

publications.title: Automatic mind wandering detection in educational settings: A systematic review and multimodal benchmarking
Every Token Needs Its Own Teacher: Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-distillation
publications.abstract: On-policy Self-distillation (OPSD) has proven effective for post-training large language models by constructing a teacher conditioned on privileged references. However, existing approaches keep the teacher fixed either throughout training by consistently exposing it to the full reference, or within each response by adaptively varying partial reference exposure only across responses. In this paper, we argue that neither of them is sufficient. Instead, every token needs its own teacher, as the teacher preference can vary token by token within the same response. Through a teacher-intervention pilot study, we validate that the teacher preference differs across tokens, and reveal that a preferred teacher can be identified for each token through majority voting and KL-based selection. Motivated by these findings, we propose Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation (MTA-OPSD), the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. Our method constructs a multi-teacher pool consisting of candidate teachers, and enables every token to adaptively select its preferred teacher during training. Experiments with Qwen3 models on mathematical reasoning tasks show that MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms existing OPSD approaches with an average gain of up to $+5.9$ over the base model, highlighting the importance of adapting teacher supervision at the token level. The code is available at https://github.com/xingzhejun/MTA-OPSD.

publications.title: When Interpretations Persist: Downstream Influence in Gaze-Aware Assistants
publications.abstract: AI assistants may carry forward not only observations but also interpretations of what a person is doing or may do next across time. Once retained, these interpretations become context for later predictions and system-triggered outputs. We study whether this representation step changes later behavior in gaze-aware streaming assistance. Holding retrieved events, their order, and the target input fixed, we find that Free-form Interpretation amplifies historical influence in both directions: correct histories produce more helpful changes and wrong histories more harmful changes. Unsupported and broader interpretations about activity or future behavior are associated with greater harmful influence. Evidence-Bounded Interpretation preserves distinctions between observation, inference, uncertainty, and temporal scope, reducing unsupported and overcertain content and lowering wrong-source harmful influence while retaining most helpful influence. The same effect structure appears with a second model. These findings identify persistent interpretation as a consequential design choice for history-aware human-AI systems.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

publications.title: User intent recognition and satisfaction with large language models: A user study with ChatGPT
publications.abstract: The rapid evolution of LLMs represents an impactful paradigm shift in digital interaction and content engagement. While they encode vast amounts of human-generated knowledge and excel in processing diverse data types, they often face the challenge of accurately responding to specific user intents, leading to user dissatisfaction. Based on a fine-grained intent taxonomy and intent-based prompt reformulations, we analyze the quality of intent recognition and user satisfaction with answers from intent-based prompt reformulations of GPT-3.5 Turbo and GPT-4 Turbo models. Our study highlights the importance of human-AI interaction and underscores the need for interdisciplinary approaches to improve conversational AI systems. We show that GPT-4 outperforms GPT-3.5 in recognizing common intents but is often outperformed by GPT-3.5 in recognizing less frequent intents. Moreover, whenever the user intent is correctly recognized, while users are more satisfied with the intent-based reformulations of GPT-4 compared to GPT-3.5, they tend to be more satisfied with the models' answers to their original prompts compared to the reformulated ones. The collected data from our study has been made publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/ConcealedIDentity/UserIntentStudy) for further research.

name: Fabian Joachim Theis
coauthors: the Human Cell Atlas Gut Bionetwork

publications.title: Multimodal cell foundation models require synergistic integration beyond alignment
publications.abstract: Abstract Integrating measurements across modalities and scales into unified quantitative frameworks of cellular function is a central goal in computational biology. Although powerful unimodal foundation models exist, the scarcity of large-scale paired data limits joint multimodal training. This constraint favours compositional foundation models, which fuse frozen unimodal experts through a learned interface. However, it remains unclear when such fusion provides task-relevant information beyond the strongest unimodal representation rather than merely aggregating redundant signal. Here we introduce Synergistic Information Score, a metric grounded in partial information decomposition that quantifies information gain arising only from cross-modal interactions. Extending theory from self-supervised learning, we show that standard alignment-based objectives with frozen encoders collapse to detect linear redundancies, which constrains their ability to capture nonlinear synergistic states. This distinction is especially important for tasks that connect tissue morphology with gene expression. Benchmarking ten fusion methods on spatial transcriptomics datasets, we demonstrate that tasks dominated by linear redundancies are well served by unimodal baselines, whereas complex niche definitions benefit from synergy-aware integration. Finally, we perform a scaling analysis and show that fine-tuning a dominant unimodal expert is the most sample-efficient strategy for standard tasks. Together, these results suggest that progress in multimodal modelling of cellular state requires shifting from alignment-based objectives to synergy-driven integration that exploits complementary cross-modal signal.

publications.title: The Human Gut Cell Atlas v1.0: A Unified, Community-Built Reference of Cellular Diversity Across the Gut
publications.abstract: Abstract Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies have transformed our understanding of cellular diversity in the human intestine, but differences in anatomical sampling, experimental processing and cell-type nomenclature limit comparison across datasets. Here, we present the Human Gut Cell Atlas (HGCA) V1, a community-curated reference of 944,390 healthy and disease-adjacent intestinal cells from 502 samples, 265 donors and 24 landmark studies, linked to detailed anatomical, clinical, and technical metadata. As this metadata is of critical importance to human biology, we developed MetaManager, an open source data management framework for standardized metadata collection and tracking. A five-level consensus taxonomy resolves 94 homeostatic cell identities and enables transferrable, high-resolution annotation of new gut datasets. By assembling cell identity, sampling metadata, and independent spatial validation, intestinal segment and radial tissue depth were revealed to systematically shape cellular composition and transcriptional state, enabling inference of the presence of sampling-dependent tissue niches, including lymphoid follicles. Reference mapping accurately and rapidly recovered cohort-level Crohn’s disease and treatment signatures without de novo annotation, while mapping human intestinal organoids quantified cell-type-specific identity, regional specification, maturation, and transcriptional fidelity to native tissue. The HGCA V1 provides a standardized cellular, anatomical coordinate, and metadata system for reproducible, high-quality analysis of intestinal biology across healthy tissue, disease-associated remodelling, and experimental models, providing a continuously evolving community reference for cumulative discovery in human intestinal biology.

publications.title: Generative inverse design steers human hematopoietic cell fate in vitro
publications.abstract: Summary Inverse design has advanced the discovery of molecules and materials. Yet it remains largely unexplored for steering cell fate, where inputs are continuous, combinatorial culture conditions and outputs are distributions of cell states. Human hematopoiesis, in which combinations and doses of growth factors steer stem cells toward each blood lineage, is a demanding test case. While forward models can evaluate discrete conditions, the vast combinatorial space renders searching for a specific, target-producing design an intractable inverse problem. Here, we introduce LabCompass, an inverse-modeling framework that optimizes experimental designs toward candidates expected to produce specified target cell states, using a flow-matching generative model guided by cellular phenotypes predicted by a forward surrogate. We applied LabCompass to primary human CD34+ in vitro cultures, where continuous cytokine and small-molecule parameters govern hematopoietic cell fate. In a lab-in-the-loop setting, we experimentally validated model-driven designs and used these measurements to update the model across four successive loops. LabCompass recovered established lineage-inducing designs, improved predictions with new data, and enriched target populations across lineages. Incorporating new parameters expanded the design space and enriched rare populations beyond initial reach. Across loops, we generated a 78-million-cell spectral flow cytometry dataset and identified distinct culture conditions converging on the same target cell states. Our results establish generative inverse modeling as a compelling paradigm for navigating high-dimensional, continuous experimental spaces, and demonstrate that virtual cell models should be judged not only by how accurately they predict cellular responses, but also by how effectively they guide experiments toward desired biological outcomes.

publications.title: SPARCS enables scalable recovery of complex image-based phenotypes for genetic screening
publications.abstract: Forward genetic screening links genotype to phenotype by introducing random genetic perturbations and identifying phenotype-altering mutations. Although genome-scale screens are routine for simple phenotypes in cultured cells, extending them to complex image-based phenotypes remains challenging. Here, we present spatially resolved CRISPR screening (SPARCS), a microscopy-based platform for forward genetic screening on single-cell images. SPARCS physically isolates mutants in situ by automated laser microdissection, enabling image-based screening at unprecedented scale with multimodal hit phenotyping. We demonstrate SPARCS in genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens of autophagosome formation and activation of the immune sensor STING across 70 million cells. Via machine learning-based image analysis, SPARCS recovered most macroautophagy genes and identified GPHR as a pH-dependent regulator of STING. Mass spectrometry-based proteomics of isolated hit cells revealed endoplasmic reticulum (ER)/Golgi disruption and nominated additional STING regulators via in silico perturbation modeling. These results establish SPARCS as a scalable platform for genome-wide genetic screening of complex cellular phenotypes with a proteome-level readout.

publications.title: ArchMap is a web-based platform for reference-based analysis of single-cell datasets
publications.abstract: Leveraging single-cell reference atlases to analyze new data has brought about a paradigm shift in single-cell data science akin to the first reference genome in genomics. However, methods for performing this mapping require computational expertise and, oftentimes, considerable compute power, limiting access for researchers who may benefit the most. Here ArchMap, a no-code query-to-reference mapping tool, removes this barrier by providing all-in-one automated mapping, cell-type annotation and collaborative features to analyze single-cell datasets from a wide range of integrated, often published, reference atlases and allows the extension of atlases with the growing Human Cell Atlas and related efforts. This paves the way for a democratization of reference mapping capabilities.

name: Fang Wang

publications.title: MAPK Signaling Pathway and Hyd Genes’ Spatiotemporal Expression Profiles in the Hypsizygus marmoreus Mycelium–Primordium–Button–Fruiting Body Transcriptome and Proteome
publications.abstract: Hypsizygus marmoreus (Peck) H.E. Bigelow is a high-quality edible fungus that is both delicious and nutritious. In this study, we conducted high-throughput transcriptomic and LC-MS/MS proteomic analyses of the H. marmoreus mycelium, primordium, button, and fruiting body developmental stages. The results revealed that gene expression in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling pathway was most significantly up- and downregulated during the primordium–button–fruiting body stages. The cell-wall stress subpathway exhibited relatively active gene expression, with a total of three pathway node genes showing upregulated expressions. During the primordium and fruiting body development stages, Hydrophobin-1, Hydrophobin-3, Hydrophobin-4, Hydrophobin-5, and Hydrophobin-6 exhibited the highest expression levels, with Hydrophobin-2 exhibiting the highest expression level during mycelium development. The expression of pathway node genes in the MAPK signaling pathway in H. marmoreus is similar with the timings of peak expressions of Hydrophobin gene family members during the primordium–button–fruiting body development stages. These results indicate that the expressions of Hydrophobin gene family members are highest during the primordium–button–fruiting body developmental stages. The expression patterns of Hydrophobin gene family members, with peaks during the primordium–button–fruiting body developmental stages and whose expression is closely linked to the period of active pathway node gene expressions in the MAPK signaling pathway. The study results will provide a solid theoretical foundation for elucidating the mechanisms underlying gene expression in the MAPK pathway in H. marmoreus.

Perspectives for expanding the assessment framework for pesticide effects on soil biodiversity
Dramatic Enhancement and Integration of Properties in Pork Belly‐Inspired All‐Biomass Composite Films via Facile, Sustainable, and Controllable Design
publications.abstract: ABSTRACT Although all‐biomass composite films that integrate electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding, thermal management, and mechanical properties are promising alternatives to conventional flexible electronic materials owing to the renewability, degradability, and sustainability, the substantial performance shortcomings severely limit the practical availability of these materials. In this study, an effective layer‐by‐layer assembly strategy inspired by the hierarchical structure of pork belly was proposed to fabricate alternating multilayer (AM) biomimetic composite films composed of cellulose nanofibers (CNFs), graphitized carbon nanosheets (GCNs), and gelatin. Efficient stress transfer, phonon transport, and electromagnetic attenuation were achieved through the construction of a robust hierarchical multilayer architecture enabled by the synergistic interactions among GCNs, CNFs, and gelatin. The results showed that the AM‐7 composite film exhibited a tensile strength of 121.20 MPa, which was increased by 266% and 199% compared with CF and CG composite films, respectively. An enhanced in‐plane thermal conductivity of 6.34 W·m − 1 ·K − 1 was achieved, and the EMI shielding effectiveness attained 56.35 dB. This work provides a sustainable strategy for the high‐value utilization of agricultural waste while offering new insights into the rational design of high‐performance multifunctional biomass‐based composites.

publications.title: Nanoplastic Size Governs the Decoupling of Microbial Survival from Antibiotic Degradation
publications.abstract: Abstract Nanoplastics (NPs) and antibiotics co-occur in wastewater systems, but how NP size influences antibiotic biodegradation by specialized degraders remains unclear. Here, we investigated the effects of europium-doped polystyrene nanoplastics (PS-NPs; PS20 and PS100) on sulfadiazine biodegradation by Arthrobacter sp. strain D2. Modified Gompertz modeling revealed two contrasting inhibition regimes. For PS100, inhibition was dominated by lag-phase prolongation, with no detectable sulfadiazine removal over 48 h at a PS100 concentration of 100 mg L–1. In contrast, PS20 reduced the maximum sulfadiazine degradation rate by ∼40% while causing only minor changes in lag time, indicating rate-dominated inhibition. Quartz crystal microbalance with dissipation monitoring at a model sulfadiazine-enriched interface showed that PS100 markedly reduced the deposition of NP-pre-exposed cells, whereas PS20 only partially impaired adhesion. Transmission electron microscopy coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy further revealed intracellular accumulation of PS20, whereas PS100 remained predominantly extracellular. Phase-specific physiological measurements and transcriptomics suggested that PS20 induced oxidative-stress responses associated with reduced sulfadiazine biodegradation rates, whereas PS100 elicited dose-dependent transcriptional changes during lag-phase extension. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that nanoplastics impair antibiotic attenuation through distinct size-dependent mechanisms involving interface-associated constraints and intracellular interference, highlighting particle size as a key determinant of antibiotic fate in plastic-contaminated wastewater environments.

name: Felix Rauscher
topics: Particle physics theoretical and experimental studies

publications.title: Unveiling the growth mode diagram of GaSe on sapphire
publications.abstract: Abstract The growth of two-dimensional epitaxial materials on industrially relevant substrates is critical for enabling their scalable synthesis and integration into next-generation technologies. Here we present a comprehensive study of the molecular beam epitaxial growth of gallium selenide on 2-inch c-plane sapphire substrates. Using in situ reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED), in situ Raman spectroscopy, optical and scanning electron microscopies, we construct a diagram of the gallium selenide growth modes as a function of substrate temperature (530–650 °C) and Se/Ga flux ratio (5–110). The growth mode diagram reveals distinct regimes, including the growth of layered post-transition metal monochalcogenide GaSe with an unstrained in-plane lattice constant of 3.71 ± 0.01 $$\dot{{{{\rm{A}}}}}$$ A ° and a partial epitaxial alignment on sapphire. This work demonstrates a RHEED-based pathway for synthesizing gallium selenide of specific phase and morphology, and the construction of a phase diagram for high vapor pressure III-VI compounds that can be applied to a wide range of other metal chalcogenide materials.

publications.title: Search for quantum black hole production in lepton+jet final states using proton-proton collisions at s=13 TeV with the ATLAS detector
publications.abstract: A search for quantum black holes in electron+jet and muon+jet invariant mass spectra is performed with 140 fb−1 of data collected by the ATLAS detector in proton-proton collisions at s=13 TeV at the Large Hadron Collider. The observed invariant mass spectrum of lepton+jet pairs is consistent with Standard Model expectations. Upper limits are set at 95% confidence level on the production cross section times branching fractions for quantum black holes decaying into a lepton and a quark in a search region with invariant mass above 2.0 TeV. The resulting quantum black hole lower mass threshold limit is 9.2 TeV in the Arkani-Hamed-Dimopoulos-Dvali model, and 6.8 TeV in the Randall-Sundrum model. © 2024 CERN, for the ATLAS Collaboration 2024 CERN
topics: Particle physics theoretical and experimental studies

publications.title: Measurement of cross sections for production of a Z boson in association with a flavor-inclusive or doubly b -tagged large-radius jet in proton-proton collisions at s=13 TeV with the ATLAS experiment
publications.abstract: We present measurements of cross sections for production of a leptonically decaying $Z$ boson in association with a large-radius jet in 13 TeV proton-proton collisions at the LHC, using $36\text{ }\text{ }{\mathrm{fb}}^{\ensuremath{-}1}$ of data from the ATLAS detector. Integrated and differential cross sections are measured at particle level in both a flavor inclusive and a doubly $b$-tagged fiducial phase space. The large-radius jet mass and transverse momentum, its kinematic relationship to the $Z$ boson, and the angular separation of $b$-tagged small-radius track jets within the large-radius jet are measured. This measurement constitutes an important test of perturbative quantum chromodynamics in kinematic and flavor configurations relevant to several Higgs boson and beyond-Standard-Model physics analyses. The results highlight issues with modeling of additional hadronic activity in the flavor-inclusive selection, and a distinction between flavor-number schemes in the $b$-tagged phase space.
topics: Particle physics theoretical and experimental studies

publications.title: Measurement of the top-quark mass using a leptonic invariant mass in pp collisions at $$ \sqrt{s} $$ = 13 TeV with the ATLAS detector
publications.abstract: Abstract A measurement of the top-quark mass (mt) in the $$ t\overline{t} $$ t t ¯ → lepton + jets channel is presented, with an experimental technique which exploits semileptonic decays of b-hadrons produced in the top-quark decay chain. The distribution of the invariant mass mℓμ of the lepton, ℓ (with ℓ = e, μ), from the W-boson decay and the muon, μ, originating from the b-hadron decay is reconstructed, and a binned-template profile likelihood fit is performed to extract mt. The measurement is based on data corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 36.1 fb−1 of $$ \sqrt{s} $$ s = 13 TeV pp collisions provided by the Large Hadron Collider and recorded by the ATLAS detector. The measured value of the top-quark mass is mt = 174.41 ± 0.39 (stat.) ± 0.66 (syst.) ± 0.25 (recoil) GeV, where the third uncertainty arises from changing the Pythia8 parton shower gluon-recoil scheme, used in top-quark decays, to a recently developed setup.
topics: Particle physics theoretical and experimental studies

publications.title: Obituary: Rupert Gerzer (1950–2025)
Differential segment‐specific signalling pathways for guanylate cyclase C‐activated anion secretion in murine ileocolon
publications.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Guanylate cyclase-C (GC-C) is the receptor for endogenous (uro)guanylin peptides, bacterial toxins and pharmacological analogues. Receptor activation leads to intestinal fluid loss, but also activates an antiproliferative pathway and is a promising target in colorectal cancer therapy. The present study delineates the molecular mechanisms that regulate the intensity of the anion secretory response (ASR) to GC-C activation in the different segments of the murine ileocolon. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: To assess the ASR to the guanylin analogue linaclotide, isolated mucosa from the different segments of the ileocolon of cGMP-dependent kinase II (cGKII)-deficient and WT mice were studied electrophysiologically in Ussing-chambers. The mucosal expression pattern of different phosphodiesterases (PDEs) was measured by RT-PCR. KEY RESULTS: The ASR to linaclotide and 8-pCPT-cGMP was strongly dependent on the presence of cGKII in the ileum and proximal colon, but not in the mid and distal colon, where cGKII expression is low. The inhibition of cGMP-sensitive PDE3 completely prevented the linaclotide-induced ASR only in the mid and distal colon, demonstrating that GC-C dependent ASR occurs via an increase in cAMP in these segments, mediated by the cGMP-induced inhibition of PDE3. In addition, the cGMP-specific PDE9 was highly expressed in the distal colon, and its inhibition strongly enhanced the ASR to linaclotide. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: GC-C activation leads to CFTR-mediated ASR in all segments of the intestine. In the mid and distal colon ASR is strongly reduced by the low cGKII and high PDE9 expression, with the CFTR channel being activated via cAMP-mediated phosphorylation.

publications.title: Article 89 Amendments to Directive 2000/31/EC
cGMP ‐dependent kinase 2, Na+/H+ exchanger NHE3, and PDZ ‐adaptor NHERF2 co‐assemble in apical membrane microdomains
publications.abstract: AIM: Exchanger Regulatory Factor (NHERF) family of PDZ-adapter proteins. This study explored the assembly of NHE3 and NHERF2 with the cGMP-dependent kinase II (cGKII) within detergent-resistant membrane microdomains (DRMs, "lipid rafts") during in vivo guanylate cycle C receptor (Gucy2c) activation in murine small intestine. METHODS: Small intestinal brush border membranes (siBBMs) were isolated from wild type, NHE3-deficient, cGMP-kinase II-deficient, and NHERF2-deficient mice, after oral application of the heat-stable Escherichia coli toxin (STa) analog linaclotide. Lipid raft and non-raft fractions were separated by Optiprep density gradient centrifugation of Triton X-solubilized siBBMs. Confocal microscopy was performed to study NHE3 redistribution after linaclotide application in vivo. RESULTS: In the WT siBBM, NHE3, NHERF2, and cGKII were strongly raft associated. The raft association of NHE3, but not of cGKII, was NHERF2 dependent. After linaclotide application to WT mice, lipid raft association of NHE3 decreased, that of cGKII increased, while that of NHERF2 did not change. NHE3 expression in the BBM shifted from a microvillar to a terminal web region. The linaclotide-induced decrease in NHE3 raft association and in microvillar abundance was abolished in cGKII-deficient mice, and strongly reduced in NHERF2-deficient mice. CONCLUSION: NHE3, cGKII, and NHERF2 form a lipid raft-associated signal complex in the siBBM, which mediates the inhibition of salt and water absorption by Gucy2c activation. NHERF2 enhances the raft association of NHE3, which is essential for its close interaction with the exclusively raft-associated activated cGKII.

publications.title: Distributed Network Sensing as an Escape Strategy
publications.abstract: The response of a swarm of ants or birds, living tissue of cells, or a robotic swarm, to spatial signals from the environment as a whole is a fundamental challenge for these decentralized systems. A promising alternative is embodied distributed sensing and decision-making, so that local environmental cues directly shape coordinated reconfiguration, growth, or movement without centralized control. Fluidic networks offer a physical basis for such systems, yet existing implementations are predesigned and limited in their ability to process spatial information across extended systems. Here, we investigate how fluid transport networks enable environmental sensing and adaptive response using the slime mould Physarum polycephalum. By exposing Physarum vein networks to dynamic pH environments, we show that the organism's ability to respond to aversive stimuli is governed by its spatial extent and network connectivity. Above a certain size, organisms with network morphology reliably detect and escape harmful conditions by network reconfiguration, whereas disconnected or spatially confined organisms fail to respond. In environments with competing stimuli, network morphologies enable integration of spatial information and repositioning into favorable regions. We identify local contractions as a physical mechanism that drives fluid redistribution and converts local stimulation into system-level responses. Finally, we generate different morphologies using fluidic and electrochemical control, demonstrating large-scale adaptation to complex environments. These results establish distributed fluidic networks as a framework for integrated sensing and actuation, providing design principles for autonomous soft robotic systems in dynamic environments.

publications.title: Experimental umbrella sampling of a rotary nanomachine
publications.abstract: Abstract The free-energy landscape of a molecular system, which describes its free energy as a function of a few collective coordinates, governs its dynamics and function, but is challenging to determine experimentally. In molecular simulations, enhanced-sampling methods such as umbrella sampling use bias potentials to access regions of this landscape that are rarely visited by equilibrium fluctuations. Here, we transfer this concept to a single-molecule experiment: we combine electric-field biasing, in situ calibration of the bias potentials, and statistical reweighting to reconstruct the angular free-energy landscapes of rotary DNA nanomachines. The method resolves barriers exceeding 10 k B T and detects changes in local landscape shape caused by small modifications of the stator design. A systematic analysis of bias calibration, sampling, and finite-exposure averaging establishes the conditions required for accurate reconstruction. Experimental umbrella sampling thus relates nanoscale structure to the underlying free-energy landscape and supports the physics-informed design of artificial molecular machinery.

publications.title: DNA Origami Nanomechanical Amplifiers for Resolving Single-Molecule Binding Events
publications.abstract: Abstract Mechanical amplification of minute length changes enables precise measurements across many orders of magnitude, from macroscopic metrology to optical instrumentation. Extending this principle to molecular systems could provide a route to monitoring nanoscale structural changes without relying on analyte labeling or fluorescence-based distance measurements. Here we present a DNA origami nanomechanical amplifier that converts subnanometre-scale molecular conformational changes into amplified mechanical displacements that can be tracked in real time at the single-molecule level. The platform resolves geometric changes associated with DNA hybridization, secondary-structure formation, DNA strand-exchange dynamics, and ligand-induced aptamer folding, enabling quantitative analysis of molecular kinetics and direct observation of transient intermediates and heterogeneous conformational ensembles. By translating molecular recognition events into mechanically amplified signals, our approach establishes a general framework for monitoring binding-coupled conformational dynamics and extends the scope of single-molecule measurements beyond conventional optical readouts.

publications.title: Magnetic DNA Origami Nanorotors
publications.abstract: Self-assembled DNA nanostructures show great promise as functional devices, highly configurable materials, and in nanorobotics. Magnetic control provides a powerful and broadly applicable actuation mechanism due to its programmability, compatibility with biological entities, and orthogonality to chemical or electrical stimuli. Here we demonstrate magnetic nanoactuators by leveraging the unique site-specificity of DNA origami to assemble magnetic nanocubes with high magnetization and magnetic anisotropy on high-aspect ratio DNA origami bundles. We trace and control 100s of our DNA origami nanorotors at the single-rotor level and demonstrate their magnetic clamping and controlled rotation under uniform and rotating magnetic fields. By varying the population and inter-particle spacing of the nanocubes, magnetic torque values on the order of 10-100 pN nm are calculated at field strengths < 10 mT. Monte Carlo simulations reveal that the assembly of nanocubes on DNA origami rotors leads to collective magnetic properties, with numerically estimated torque values in good agreement with the experiments. Our work demonstrates a proof-of-concept of nanoscale magnetic actuators for potential uses as programmable torque nano-probes and in nanorobotics.

publications.title: A high-endurance DNA origami snap-through switch for functional nanoscale control
publications.abstract: Switchable elements are central to both technological devices and biological machines because they enable controlled and reversible transitions between distinct functional states. Here, we present a DNA origami-based, mechanically bistable snap-through mechanism that can be electrically controlled. This nanoscale switching mechanism exhibits long-term stability in both states in the absence of external stimuli while achieving millisecond-scale switching times upon application of an electric field. Individual devices sustain hundreds of thousands of switching cycles over several hours and remain functional for actuation over several days, offering a powerful platform for systematically studying the endurance and failure mechanisms of biomolecular nanoswitches. As a nanoscale electromechanical interface, our device enables applications in molecular information processing, optical nanodevices, and the dynamic control of chemical reactions. We demonstrate that functionalization with gold nanorods facilitates polarization-dependent optical modulation, establishing direct application in plasmonics. We further show that controlling the accessibility of a molecular binding site allows electrical regulation of reaction kinetics, thereby directly coupling mechanical switching to biochemical function.

publications.title: Verbundprojekt: 6G-TERAKOM; Teilvorhaben Synchronisation für THz-Kommunikationssysteme mit 1-bit Quantisierung
publications.abstract: For future wireless communications systems targeting data rates of 1 Tbit/s and beyond, utilizing very high bandwidths at sub-terahertz frequencies, reducing the analogto-digital converter (ADC) resolution to 1 bit is a promising solution to limit receiver power consumption.With 1-bit quantization being a highly non-linear operation, conventional receiver synchronization algorithms cannot be directly applied, which includes timing and phase synchronization.In this paper we focus on the estimation and compensation of unknown timing and phase offsets between the transmitter and the receiver.To this end, a synchronization approach is proposed, which is able to operate on receive samples with 1-bit amplitude resolution and comprises a least squares (LS) timing estimator, a digital timing synchronizer based on interpolation and decimation, an LS phase estimator utilizing the outputs of the timing synchronizer, and a finite-resolution analog phase shifter at the receiver for phase offset compensation.Evaluating the system performance in terms of achievable rate using zero-crossing modulation (ZXM), we find that the proposed LS estimators in combination with the employed synchronization scheme enable to achieve rates very close to those obtained with known timing and phase offsets, with reasonably small pilot overhead.Moreover, we find that when using ZXM with higher faster-than-Nyquist factors the system becomes more sensitive to estimation errors, necessitating longer pilot sequences, whereas phase synchronization with a low-resolution phase shifter is sufficient to closely approach the performance of an ideal phase shifter.
topics: Advancements in PLL and VCO Technologies

publications.title: Spectrum Anomaly Detection in OFDMA Systems: Simulation Framework and Benchmark Dataset
publications.abstract: Overview This dataset accompanies the paper Spectrum Anomaly Detection in OFDMA Systems: Simulation Framework and Benchmark Dataset and serves as a benchmark for spectrum anomaly detection. It is generated by simulating an OFDMA network in an industrial indoor environment, with propagation modeled via ray tracing. It consists of 20,000 samples, each with spectrograms from 21 spatially distributed sensing units (SUs), a resource allocation map, and labels. Half of the samples are normal, the other half contain one of five jammer types (2,000 samples each), ranging from noise-like to deceptive jamming. Predefined splits for supervised and unsupervised learning are included. Generation, file formats, labels, and splits are documented in detail in the repository README. Related links Preprint: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.02102 GitHub: https://github.com/akdd11/ofdma-spectrum-anomalies-simulation API documentation: https://akdd11.github.io/ofdma-spectrum-anomalies-simulation/ Files File Content images.zip Spectrograms spectrogram-<sample_idx>-<su_idx>.png and resource allocation grids alloc_res-<sample_idx>.png labels.csv Labels, jammer impact metrics, and data splits, one row per sample spectrogram_min_max.csv Clipping bounds in dB, to rescale the 8-bit values su_coordinates.csv SU positions in m su_hardware.csv Per-SU hardware impairment parameters config.yaml Full configuration of the generation run Sample indices are ordered by class: samples 0–9999 are normal, followed by blocks of 2,000 samples of the jammer types deceptive, sweep, barrage, pilot, and random_hop. Spectrograms: 8-bit grayscale PNGs with one pixel per resource element (1320 subcarriers × 70 OFDM symbols). All spectrograms share the same clipping bounds; a pixel value v corresponds to min_val + v / 255 * (max_val - min_val) dB. The spectrograms include receiver hardware impairments of the SUs (IQ imbalance, DC offset, residual timing and frequency offsets). Resource allocation: 8-bit PNGs of the same resolution, where 0 means not allocated and any other value is the index of the allocated transmitter. Since the values are small, the images look almost black, but the information is there. Labels: jammer type, power, and location; number of legitimate transmitters; per-SU SNR and SJR; jammer occupancy, local JSNR, and dB contrast as measures of jammer impact; and the columns split_supervised and split_unsupervised (train/valid/test). For normal samples, the jammer-related columns are NaN, except for the SJR, which is inf. Changes from version 1.0 Version 2.0 has been regenerated with an updated simulation framework. Results on the two versions are not directly comparable. Simulation: per-SU receiver hardware impairments, wedge diffraction in ray tracing, channel applied as band-limited taps (fixes out-of-band leakage), random modulation order (QPSK/16-QAM/64-QAM) per transmitter, and seeded random draws for reproducibility. Spectrograms: clipped to a dataset-wide range before 8-bit scaling, instead of min-max scaling over the full value range. labels.csv: jammer location split into jammer_x, jammer_y, jammer_z; new jammer impact metrics and split columns. New files: su_coordinates.csv, su_hardware.csv, config.yaml.
