topics: Food Nutrient Composition and Product Development

publications.title: Datasets, Processing Workflows and Analysis Code for Integrated High-Content Screening and FT-ICR-MS Metabolomics of Probiotic-Conditioned Media
publications.abstract: This repository contains the datasets, data processing workflows, analysis scripts, and plotting code associated with the study entitled "From Metabolites to Morphology: Conjugated and Deconjugated Bile Acids as Candidate Metabolites Associated with Probiotic-Induced Morphological Changes." The study integrates high-resolution Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR-MS), targeted liquid chromatography time-of-flight mass spectrometry (LC-TOF-MS), and high-content screening (HCS) to investigate extracellular metabolite profiles from 46 probiotic strains and their associations with morphological responses in Caco-2 and HT-1080 cells. The repository is organized into three main directories: Datasets: Contains available raw and processed datasets, including 16 dataset configurations used to investigate different preprocessing strategies, feature selection approaches, and statistical models. The repository also includes HCS measurements, FT-ICR-MS metabolomics data, and LC-TOF-MS bile acid measurements. Scripts: Contains Python-based workflows for data preprocessing, normalization, multivariate statistical analysis, and integration of metabolomic and morphological data. The analyses include principal component analysis (PCA), hierarchical clustering, correlation analysis, partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), partial least squares regression (PLSR), and LASSO regression. Plots: Contains scripts and supporting materials used to generate the main figures and supplementary visualizations presented in the manuscript. The targeted LC-TOF-MS analysis investigated unconjugated and glycine-conjugated bile acids using authentic reference standards. Bile acid identification was supported by accurate mass measurements and chromatographic retention times, with UDCA and HDCA reported jointly because these isomers could not be chromatographically resolved. The statistical modeling workflows were developed for exploratory metabolite prioritization rather than independently validated prediction. The identified associations between metabolite profiles and cellular morphology should therefore be interpreted as hypothesis-generating and not as evidence of direct causality. The deposited materials support transparency, reproducibility, and further investigation of metabolite-associated cellular responses to probiotic-conditioned media.

publications.title: Post‐flight assessment of the OSIRIS ‐ REx Sample Return Capsule ( SRC ) for organic and other potential contaminants
publications.abstract: Abstract Regolith samples from the carbonaceous asteroid Bennu were stowed and delivered to Earth in the OSIRIS‐REx spacecraft's Sample Return Capsule (SRC). We applied multiple analytical techniques to study the components of the post‐flight SRC, with a focus on assessing the conditions and any contaminants to which the Bennu samples were exposed. Examination of the passive temperature sensors placed inside the SRC, in combination with thermal modeling results, indicate that the samples were not heated above the 75°C limit imposed by OSIRIS‐REx mission requirements. The sample canister air filter was found to contain Bennu particulates that had escaped from the sample collector, as well as a range of contaminants likely associated with the original filter component materials. No indications of terrestrial soils were found in the filter. Isotopic analyses of organic compounds and noble gases trapped in the filter show values consistent with terrestrial origins, and there are no indications of trapped asteroidal volatiles. Organic compounds found in the flight filter that were not present in a non‐flight control filter include aromatic hydrocarbons, alkylated aromatic hydrocarbons, phenolic‐related compounds, aliphatic hydrocarbons, and alcohols. The abundances of these organic compounds typically decrease from outer layers of the filter toward the canister interior, suggesting that they are external contaminants. We conclude that the majority of these organic compounds are chemical byproducts associated with outgassing of the SRC heatshield and backshell following the ablation portion of SRC atmospheric entry. Overall, our findings show that the OSIRIS‐REx SRC performed excellently in containerizing the asteroidal samples obtained at Bennu, delivering them safely to the ground at the UTTR, and preventing most, though perhaps not all, external contaminants from reaching them. We discuss lessons learned from the flight and recovery of the OSIRIS‐REx SRC that can benefit future sample return missions.

publications.title: OSIRIS-REx Returned a Pristine Sample of Asteroid Bennu: Takeaways from the Mission's Contamination Control and Knowledge Program
publications.abstract: NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission had the objective of delivering a pristine sample from asteroid (101955) Bennu to Earth for scientific analysis--where "pristine" signifies the absence of foreign materials that could affect sample measurements. OSIRIS-REx returned 121.6 g of regolith in September 2023; this study documents the systematic investigation of suspected contaminants encountered during the mission's sample analysis phase. Most suspected contaminants did not originate from the spacecraft or sample curation. Some were introduced during laboratory analyses, reinforcing the importance of procedural blanks and a strategic approach to sharing samples across laboratories with different analytical targets. Several suspected contaminants, such as phosphate and sodium fluoride particles, were ultimately identified as indigenous to Bennu, highlighting the critical role of contamination knowledge in preventing the dismissal of valuable scientific data. We find that the returned sample meets the definition of pristine, except for an isolated 1.24% (by mass) that escaped the sample container and was thereby contaminated with spacecraft particulates. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of systematically applied contamination science and engineering practices and provide lessons and approaches to help maximize the scientific integrity of future planetary sample return missions.

publications.title: Corrigendum to “Metabolomic profile of edible Amazonian Arecaceae fruits by FT-ICR-MS: Insights into chemical, nutritional and antioxidant profiles” [Food Chem. 525 (2026) 150319]
topics: Food Nutrient Composition and Product Development

publications.title: Comparison of Orbitrap and Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry for the analysis of dissolved organic matter
A Theory of Network Equivalence – Part II: Multiterminal Channels
publications.abstract: A technique for bounding the capacities of networks of independent channels is introduced. Parts I and II treat point-to-point and multiterminal channels, respectively. Bounds are derived using a new tool called a bounding model. Channel 1 is an upper (lower) bounding model for channel 2 if replacing channel 2 by channel 1 in any network yields a new network whose capacity region is a superset (subset) of the capacity region of the original network. This paper derives bounding models from noiseless links, with lower bounding models corresponding to points in the channel's capacity region and upper bounding models corresponding to points in a new channel characterization called an emulation region. Replacing all channels in a network by their noiseless upper (lower) bounding models yields a network of lossless links whose capacity region is a superset (subset) of the capacity region for the original network. This converts a general (often stochastic) network into a network coding instance, enabling the application of tools and results derived in that domain. A channel's upper and lower bounding models differ when the channel can carry more information in some networks than in others. Bounding the difference between upper and lower bounding models bounds both the accuracy of the technique and the price of separating source-network coding from channel coding.

publications.title: A Factorized Variational Technique for Phase Unwrapping in Markov Random Fields
publications.abstract: Some types of medical and topographic imaging device produce images in which the pixel values are "phase-wrapped", i.e. measured modulus a known scalar. Phase unwrapping can be viewed as the problem of inferring the number of shifts between each and every pair of neighboring pixels, subject to an a priori preference for smooth surfaces, and subject to a zero curl constraint, which requires that the shifts must sum to 0 around every loop. We formulate phase unwrapping as a mean field inference problem in a Markov network, where the prior favors the zero curl constraint. We compare our mean field technique with the least squares method on a synthetic 100x100 image, and give results on a 512x512 synthetic aperture radar image from Sandia National Laboratories.

publications.title: Scheduling for Network-Coded Multicast
publications.abstract: We consider multicasting using random linear network coding over a multihop wireless network in the bandwidth limited regime. We address the associated medium access problem and propose a scheduling technique that activates hyperarcs rather than links, as in classical scheduling approaches. We encapsulate the constraints on valid network configurations in a conflict graph model and formulate a joint optimization problem taking into account both the network coding subgraph and the schedule. Next, using Lagrangian relaxation, we decompose the overall problem into two subproblems, a multiple-shortest-paths problem and a maximum weighted stable set (MWSS) problem. We show that if we use a greedy heuristic for the MWSS part of the problem, the overall algorithm is completely distributed. We provide extensive simulation results for both the centralized optimal and the decentralized algorithms. The optimal algorithm improves performance by up to a factor of two over widely used techniques such as orthogonal or two-hop-constrained scheduling. The decentralized algorithm is shown to buy its distributed operation with some throughput losses. Experimental results on randomly generated networks suggest that these losses are not large. Finally, we study the power consumption of our scheme and quantify the tradeoff between power and bandwidth efficiency.

publications.title: Helpers for Cleaning Dirty Papers
VLSI Architectures for Soft-Decision Decoding of Reed–Solomon Codes
publications.abstract: Soft-decision decoding of Reed-Solomon codes delivers significant coding gains over classical minimum distance decoding. In this paper, we present architectures for polynomial interpolation and factorization, the two main steps of the soft-decoding algorithm. We introduce an algorithmic transformation for reducing the iterations required in generating the interpolation polynomial and present efficient architectures by sharing computations. We also describe algorithmic transformations for further reducing the interpolation and factorization latency. An area efficient, folded-pipelined version of the interpolation architecture is also described. Finally, we present an example of a Reed-Solomon soft decoder utilizing the presented architectures, having a 250 Mbps throughput.

publications.title: A Dual-Terminator Window for 40 m Long-Path SSB Contacts Between Germany and New Zealand
publications.abstract: Morning 7 MHz long-path single-sideband (SSB) contacts between southern Germany and New Zealand are sparse and cluster about one hour after civil dawn in Germany, although weaker signals can be received much earlier. We use archived Weak Signal Propagation Reporter (WSPR) signal-to-noise ratios for 2023–2025, audited for transmitter and receiver activity, together with semi-empirical absorption estimates and PHaRLAP ray tracing, to investigate this narrow interval. WSPR was decoded on 498 of 594 mornings with demonstrated station activity (84%). Published speech requirements and an indicative 500 W link budget narrow the 87 min WSPR detection window to an SSB-equivalent interval of 40–60 min, peaking 60–75 min after dawn, consistent with the timing of 60 documented SSB contacts. Modeled D-region absorption is lowest in this interval, when the Sun is low at both ends of the path, a dual-terminator window. The modeled minimum occurs a median of 15 min after the temporal midpoint between German civil dawn and New Zealand receiver sunset (r = 0.99, 512 mornings); because both times shift together on this nearly antipodal path, the season predicts contact time as well as dawn does. Receivers in Australia show that the window closes at receiver sunset or about 154 min after German dawn, whichever comes first. No systematic difference in closure time was detected between 7 and 10 MHz near New Zealand sunset, which argues against both absorption and a falling maximum usable frequency as the cause; the mechanism remains unresolved.

publications.title: Data and code for A Dual-Terminator Window for 40 m Long-Path SSB Contacts Between Germany and New Zealand
publications.abstract: This record contains the data and analysis code supporting the study "A Dual-Terminator Window for 40 m Long-Path SSB Contacts Between Germany and New Zealand" by Reinhard Niessner (submitted to Radio Science). It includes archived WSPR query exports (WSPRnet via WSPR.live), transmitter-receiver activity audits, morning classifications and window statistics for 2023-2025, SSB contact comparison tables, semi-empirical (George & Bradley) absorption calculations, PHaRLAP 4.7.4 grid-generation and ray-tracing scripts with numerical results for five selected mornings, the 7/10 MHz comparison, hourly Dst (WDC Kyoto via OMNI2) and the CW Doppler block and window values of the controlled series. The README identifies the source data, software requirements, licenses and the files behind each figure and table. PHaRLAP and MATLAB are not redistributed and must be obtained from their providers.

publications.title: Observational Constraints on Transient F-Region Access During 40 m Germany-New Zealand Long-Path Propagation
publications.abstract: Most of the morning Germany-New Zealand long path lies in darkness, but usable 40 m SSB propagation remains intermittent. We evaluate whether usability is associated with a transient combination of European F-region structure, loss conditions, and launch geometry rather than with a single ionospheric threshold. Sixty successful-contact rows represent 58 independent mornings. At morning level, the first documented contact occurs a median 60.0 min after civil-twilight onset (bootstrap 95% confidence interval 53.5-66.0 min) and follows its seasonal displacement. However, a harmonic day-of-year model predicts contact time at least as well in leave-one-out testing as twilight time alone, so the timing relation is descriptive and does not independently identify a twilight-controlled mechanism. Two temporally separated observational series comprising 27 strictly classified mornings show that no individual variable or enumerated one- to three-variable model transfers robustly between series. Late hmF2 descent is the strongest descriptive marker (AUC = 0.701, p = 0.085), whereas cross-series and leave-one-out multivariate performance remains near chance. For the confirmed 12 April 2026 contact, PHaRLAP-2D at 258 degrees azimuth demonstrates viable low-elevation first returns from 12 degrees upward. An independent PHaRLAP-3D homing calculation at a different azimuth identifies a 9.00-degree trajectory that spans 21,850 km in three ground hops and terminates 29.6 km from ZL1KVA. Because both calculations use an unassimilated IRI-2020 background and do not represent the same ray, they establish complementary geometrical plausibility rather than event-specific causality. The observations therefore constrain, but do not confirm, a transient multicomponent access hypothesis for documented 40 m SSB usability.

publications.title: Ionospheric Conditions Governing Grayline-Related HF Propagation Enhancement
publications.abstract: Grayline (terminator‑adjacent) HF propagation has been exploited operationally for decades, yet its predictability remains limited when defined purely by solar geometry. In this study, we investigate the role of the ionospheric state during grayline transitions using equivalent slab thickness (EST), derived from co‑located total electron content (TEC) and ionosonde peak density (NmF2 via foF2). We combine WSPR spot statistics on the 40 m band from transmissions by DK3TG (Germany) with ionosonde and TEC‑based parameters (foF2, hmF2, TEC, EST) referenced to Juliusruh and relate these diagnostics to long‑distance HF propagation toward North America and New Zealand. The results show that successful long‑distance links are not uniformly distributed across the geometrically defined grayline interval but occur within shorter time windows characterized by rapid F‑region restructuring. WSPR observations indicate that changes in EST mark the onset of propagation, whereas successful SSB communication occurs later, during a phase characterized by decreasing hmF2. For the transatlantic path, the majority of detected links occur after the grayline passage, indicating that optimal propagation conditions develop during the post‑grayline phase rather than within the grayline itself. EST provides a diagnostic of propagation onset, while the subsequent evolution of hmF2 controls the usability of the propagation channel.

publications.title: Abstract A110: Proteasome inhibitor (PI) ADC: A novel broad spectrum payload platform
publications.abstract: Abstract Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) are a therapeutic modality that combines the targeting precision of monoclonal antibodies with the potent cytotoxicity of small-molecule drugs. Despite recent progress of ADC technology in treatment of cancer, efficacy and safety profile of ADCs is often limited by the characteristics of the payloads, highlighting the need for continued innovation in payload selection strategies. To address the unmet needs, we developed a novel class of ADC payload platform employing a novel payload class that disrupts proteostasis by inhibiting a critical component of the cellular protein degradation machinery. Upon internalization, the proteasome inhibitor (PI) payload can block tumor specific protein degradation pathway such as inhibitor of kappa B (IkB) degradation in hematologic malignancies or can induce the accumulation of misfolded and damaged proteins, leading to apoptotic cell death- particularly effective in tumor cells with high protein turnover. Various antibodies were conjugated with PI payload using different conjugation technologies, generating PI-ADCs for the treatment of solid tumors or hematologic malignancies. The resulting ADCs demonstrated efficient intracellular delivery and payload-dependent activity. Strong in vitro cytotoxicity and robust in vivo anti-tumor efficacy were observed across multiple preclinical tumor models, including those with limited sensitivity to existing ADC therapies. These findings highlight the potential of a new broad spectrum payload class to overcome resistance mechanisms and expand the therapeutic landscape of ADCs across diverse malignancies. Citation Format: Won-Gyun Ahn, Jaehee Jang, Seung-Joo Lee, Yong Soo Kim, Jaeseung Kim, Robert Huber, Uwe Koch, Johannes Bange, Martin Huber, Bert Klebl, Kiyean Nam. Proteasome inhibitor (PI) ADC: A novel broad spectrum payload platform [abstract]. In: Proceedings of the AACR-NCI-EORTC International Conference on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics; 2025 Oct 22-26; Boston, MA. Philadelphia (PA): AACR; Mol Cancer Ther 2025;24(10 Suppl):Abstract nr A110.

publications.title: A Photocaged N ‐Phosphonopiperidinone as a Selective Photo‐Cleavable DPP8/9 Inhibitor
publications.abstract: The strategic introduction of photocages into chemical probes represents a powerful approach to generate spatiotemporally controlled tools with promising applications in chemical biology and drug discovery. This approach is particularly useful for inhibitors of proteins with cell-type-dependent functions, as they enable, via light-triggered selection, the study of their function in selected cells within multicellular organisms. The intracellular dipeptidyl peptidases 8 and 9 (DPP8/9) are serine hydrolases that act in a cell type-dependent fashion, in diverse biological processes such as inflammation and tumorigenesis. So far, no photocaged inhibitors for DPP8/9 are available, thus hampering their systematic investigations in biomedical research model systems such as mice. Herein, the development of a green light-cleavable, BODIPY-photocaged N-phosphono-piperidone-based DPP8/9 inhibitor is presented. This covalent-acting inhibitor is characterized by its photolysis properties, including a demonstration of its low phototoxicity, as well as potency and selectivity, in biochemical, biological, and, as an extension to these traditional validation approaches, chemical proteomics assays. These studies not only reveal the suitability of the developed photocages for cellular applications, as a prerequisite for their application in multicellular organisms, but also highlight the benefit of chemical proteomics workflows such as activity-based protein profiling for characterizing proteome-wide potencies and selectivities of photocaged compounds.

publications.title: Rational correction of pathogenic conformational defects in HTRA1
publications.abstract: Abstract Loss-of-function mutations in the homotrimeric serine protease HTRA1 cause cerebral vasculopathy. Here, we establish independent approaches to achieve the functional correction of trimer assembly defects. Focusing on the prototypical R274Q mutation, we identify an HTRA1 variant that promotes trimer formation thus restoring enzymatic activity in vitro. Genetic experiments in Htra1R274Q mice further demonstrate that expression of this protein-based corrector in trans is sufficient to stabilize HtrA1-R274Q and restore the proteomic signature of the brain vasculature. An alternative approach employs supramolecular chemical ligands that shift the monomer-trimer equilibrium towards proteolytically active trimers. Moreover, we identify a peptidic ligand that activates HTRA1 monomers. Our findings open perspectives for tailored protein repair strategies.

publications.title: Epilogue: ‘Did You Know?’ (that you are likely to be awarded the Nobel Prize)
Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis–like hyperinflammation due to a de novo mutation in DPP9

name: Roland A. Fischer
topics: Synthesis and characterization of novel inorganic/organometallic compounds

publications.title: Controlling Polymorphism and Particle Size in Zr‐Based Metal‐Organic Frameworks Through Preformed Nodes and Machine‐Learning‐Assisted Synthesis
publications.abstract: ABSTRACT Framework topology and particle size jointly govern pore architecture, diffusion limitations, and accessible surface area, making their simultaneous control essential for functional metal–organic framework (MOF) design. Achieving reproducible control over both remains a central challenge in MOF chemistry, particularly for systems capable of crystallizing in multiple polymorphs. Here, we systematically explore the synthesis of two Zr‐based MOFs, NU‐1000 and NU‐901, which share the same Zr 6 ‐oxo cluster and pyrene‐tetrabenzoate linker but differ in topology. To remove variability arising from in situ precursor formation, we employed preformed Zr 6 ‐oxo clusters as well‐defined nodes. Building on this controlled starting point, multiple particle‐size regimes (<100 nm to ∼1 µm) were accessed through systematic variation of modulator identity and loading, co‐modulator content, linker equivalents, temperature, and dilution. Machine‐learning (ML) analysis quantitatively disentangles the multivariate influences governing phase selection and particle‐size evolution. This integrated approach enables predictive navigation of the synthesis parameter space, providing reproducible access to MOFs with defined size regimes and controlled topology. Together, these results establish a generalizable experimental‐computational workflow that transforms empirical MOF synthesis into a predictable, designable process, enabling rational control over polymorphism and growth in structurally adaptable framework materials.

publications.title: In-Situ Visualization of Thermal Transformation Pathways in Leaf-Shaped Zeolitic Imidazolate Framework Derived Nanocarbon
publications.abstract: Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are versatile precursors for nanostructured, heteroatom-doped carbons. However, understanding the spatiotemporally resolved mechanisms that govern crystalline-to-amorphous framework collapse, diffusion-mediated reorganization of transient intermediates, and the subsequent formation of graphitic carbon remains challenging. Here, we elucidate the transformation of the 2D leaf-shaped zeolitic imidazolate framework ZIF-L into Zn-dispersed N-doped carbon using a combination of in situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD). These measurements directly capture the sequential collapse of the layered MOF framework and the associated morphological evolution under controlled heating, decoupled from beam-induced effects during electron microscopy. Complementary ex-situ pyrolysis (700-1100 °C), together with high-resolution TEM, synchrotron X-ray pair distribution function (X-PDF) analysis, and electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS), reveals the diffusion of Zn-containing species, ligand decomposition, and progressive graphitization within the amorphous matrix. We identify temperature-dependent stages involving ligand breakdown, migration of Zn-Nx species, followed by Zn loss, and ultimately forming porous N-doped carbon at 1000 °C that exhibits the strongest electrochemical response within this series. These findings establish temperature-dependent structure-property relationships that enable the thermal engineering of MOF-derived ORR catalysts.

publications.title: From Dark Photocatalysis to Photobattery‐Type Operation: A Re‐Functionalized Ti‐MOF for Solar Energy Storage
publications.abstract: ABSTRACT Efficient harvesting, storage, and on‐demand release of solar energy are essential for overcoming the intermittency of sunlight and enabling continuous solar energy‐driven processes, yet achieving storage of photogenerated charge remains challenging. Here, we report a Ti‐based bipyridine MOF, COK47‐bpy, and its ReCl(CO) 3 ‐functionalized analogue, ReCl47‐bpy , as photochargeable materials for time‐decoupled solar energy utilization. Re incorporation introduces localized photosensitizing and “electron sink” sites while preserving the parent framework structure, enabling visible‐light response, faster charge accumulation, and improved charge retention. In colloidal suspension, ReCl47‐bpy reaches an electron storage capacity of 19.5 C g −1 MOF under simulated solar irradiation and retains about 70% of the stored charge after 2.5 months. The stored electrons can be released on demand for dark hydrogen (H 2 ) evolution with electron‐to‐H 2 efficiencies exceeding 90%. Beyond colloids, when fabricated as robust FTO‐supported layers, ReCl47‐bpy |FTO photoelectrodes deliver capacities of up to ∼7.0 mAh g −1 MOF upon photocharging under 1 Sun irradiation. Overall, this work establishes Re‐functionalized Ti‐MOFs as versatile platforms for solar‐driven charge storage, dark photocatalysis, and MOF‐based photoelectrodes, toward the development of next‐generation MOF‐based energy devices.

publications.title: Mapping Solid Electrolyte Interphase Evolution and Lithium Deposition at Solid-State Interfaces by Operando Nano-focus WAXS
publications.abstract: Abstract Composite solid polymer electrolytes (CSPEs) have emerged as promising candidates for next-generation lithium metal batteries. However, the spatial evolution of the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) at solid-state interfaces remains poorly understood despite its critical role in lithium metal stability. Herein, the anion-trapping layered double hydroxide (LDH) is introduced to poly(ethylene oxide)-based CSPEs to regulate Li+ transport and stabilize the lithium/electrolyte interface. The LDH-enhanced electrolyte achieves exceptional cycling stability over 950 h with a lithium electrode and 90.1% capacity retention after 250 cycles in LiFePO4||Li full cells. Operando nano-focus wide-angle X-ray scattering maps the spatial distributions of both the SEI and lithium dendrites at the lithium/electrolyte interface across micron-scale lateral and vertical dimensions. The regulated Li+ flux promotes homogeneous lithium deposition and the formation of a robust, multifunctional SEI, thereby suppressing lithium dendrite growth and stabilizing the interface. This study provides direct visualization of SEI evolution in CSPEs and clarifies its role in dendrite-free all-solid-state lithium metal batteries.

publications.title: A porous and photoactive perylene diimide-based metal-organic framework for the selective oxidation of sulfides to sulfoxides
publications.abstract: Making chemical transformations more sustainable is an important goal in modern chemistry, driving the development of more efficient and environmentally friendly methodologies. The selective oxidation of sulfides to sulfoxides is an utilized transformation in pharmaceuticals and fine chemicals, yet conventional methods often require stoichiometric oxidants and generate unwanted waste. Herein, a porous PDI-based metal–organic framework, [Cd(tpda)(DMA)(H 2 O)] (Cdtpda), constructed from 1,6,7,12-tetrachloroperylenediimide-N,N′-diacetic acid and Cd 2+ nodes, is reported as a visible-light-responsive photosensitizer for sustainable sulfide oxidation. Cdtpda features three-dimensional nanosheets connected via π–π interactions, creating continuous pores, and exhibits broad UV/Vis absorption and complete fluorescence quenching, indicative of strong H-type aggregation and efficient photoinduced electron transfer. Under visible-light irradiation and molecular oxygen, Cdtpda selectively converts aryl sulfides to sulfoxides with high yield and minimal overoxidation, while remaining recyclable and structurally intact. Mechanistic investigations, including reactive oxygen species scavenging and EPR spectroscopy, reveal that this high selectivity is governed by singlet oxygen generated via photosensitization as the dominant reactive species. These findings encourage further exploration of structural diversity in PDI-based MOFs and the development of additional applications.

name: Rosa María Román-Cuesta
topics: Land use, land-use change and forestry

publications.title: The LULUCF Data Hub: regional- and national-level discrepancies between independent global datasets and national GHG inventories.
publications.abstract: Land use plays a critical role in achieving the Paris Agreement goals, yet inconsistencies between global carbon models, Earth Observation (EO), and national greenhouse gas inventories (NGHGIs) lead to significant mismatches in CO₂ emission estimates. NGHGIs, reported by countries using IPCC guidelines, guide national policies, while global models and satellite-based Earth Observation estimates support independent evaluations. Ensuring comparability among these datasets is essential.Here we introduce the LULUCF Data Hub, an interactive platform hosted by the EU Forest Observatory to visualize CO₂ emissions and removals as reported by countries to the UNFCCC, alongside independent global land-use emission datasets. NGHGI data indicate a global net LULUCF sink of -2.3 Gt CO₂ yr⁻¹ (on average 2000-2023), with declining deforestation emissions and increasing forest sinks. For total LULUCF, a good agreement emerges between the translated results from the Global Carbon Budget (GCB 2024, representing the modelling scientific community) and NGHGIs at global level, both in magnitude – with the original gap of 7.2 Gt CO2 yr-1 (2000-2022 average) reduced to 0.8 Gt CO2 yr-1 – and trend. When combining estimates for forest and deforestation, the translated results from Global Forest Watch (GFW, representing the EO scientific community in this study) also show a similar magnitude than NGHGI, but a divergent trend.While the translation methodology used here effectively addresses conceptual differences among the studied datasets at the global level and for most countries, we highlight regions and countries where disagreements in estimates persist. We provide insights into possible reasons for these discrepancies and indicate areas where further research is warranted. The ultimate objective of the LULUCF data hub is to stimulate dialogue and foster collaborative efforts across different communities to reach a greater consensus on the magnitude and trends of land use emissions and removals, in support of the implementation of the Paris Agreement and in anticipation of the next UNFCCC Global Stocktake.

publications.title: The LULUCF Data Hub: translating global land use emissions estimates into the national GHG inventory framework
publications.abstract: Abstract. Global estimates of anthropogenic land use CO2 fluxes from bookkeeping models and dynamic global vegetation models, as well as those derived from Earth observations (EO), can differ widely from those obtained by aggregation of national GHG inventories (NGHGI). These discrepancies are mostly due to conceptual differences, reflecting varying definitions (or system boundaries) of anthropogenic CO2 fluxes, particularly on the forest carbon sink. This study presents a new online platform ‒ the "LULUCF Data Hub" ‒ which compiles various datasets of country-level CO2 emissions and removals from land use, land-use change and forestry (LULUCF). Through a multi-disciplinary collaboration, results from two key global initiatives ‒ one based on carbon cycle modelling (Global Carbon Budget, GCB 2024) and one on Earth Observations (Global Forest Watch, GFW 2024) ‒ are "translated" to conceptually align with NGHGI definitions. We compared these global approaches to the 2024 NGHGI data submitted to the UNFCCC under the Paris Agreement reporting rules (cut-off date April 2025). The aim is to enhance comparability and foster consensus on anthropogenic land-use CO2 flux estimates. Translating definitions between datasets considerably improves the match in land use CO2 flux estimates, both globally and for most countries. At the global level, NGHGI indicate that LULUCF is a net sink of -3.4 Gt CO2 yr-1 (2001–2023 average; 2023 estimate is an extrapolation for all NGHGI), whereas GCB reports a net source of +4.7 Gt CO2 yr-1. This +8.1 Gt CO2 yr-1 discrepancy drops to +1.8 Gt CO2 yr-1 when GCB fluxes are translated to NGHGI definitions. When the global net forest-related flux of -5.8 Gt CO2 yr-1 estimated by the GFW model (sum of fluxes from Forest and Deforestation including organic soils) is limited to a proxy of managed forest area, the sink declines to -3.5 Gt CO2 yr-1, closely aligning with NGHGI (-3.2 Gt CO2 yr-1 for forest-related flux only, including Forest, Deforestation, and organic soils in Indonesia). Despite improved alignment in magnitude after translation, some differences persist in global CO2 flux trends: in the last two decades, forests (including re/afforestation) have remained a roughly constant net sink in NGHGI and GCB but are a declining net sink in GFW; deforestation emissions are stable or slightly declining in NGHGI and GCB but increase in GFW. For other land uses, NGHGI globally reports a greater sink than GCB (the GFW model does not include other land uses). At the country-level, we identify both convergences and divergences in CO2 flux estimates between NGHGI and the translated datasets – in sign, magnitude and trend. Notably, after translation, estimates of both GCB and GFW still differ from individual NGHGI values in 19 countries by more than ±0.1 Gt CO2 yr-1 on average (2001–2023), highlighting areas that deserve further investigation. The LULUCF Data Hub was first presented in July 2024 during the IPCC Expert Meeting on Reconciling Anthropogenic Land Use Emissions, showing preliminary data. In November 2024 version 1.0 (with NGHGI pre-Paris reporting, GCB 2024 data and GFW 2024 data) was launched. Our study shows results from version 2.0, corresponding to 2024 data from all datasets: i) NGHGI data from the first Biennial Transparency Reports (BTRs) submitted under the Paris Agreement (cut-off date April 2025), complemented by previous reports (from version 1.0) for countries with no BTR submission, ii) data from GCB 2024 and iii) data from the GFW carbon flux model 2024. Data from all versions, including future annual updates, can be visualized and downloaded from the LULUCF Data Hub hosted by the European Union Forest Observatory (European Commission Joint Research Centre, 2025) and from the online repository (Melo et al., 2025; available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17140775).

publications.title: The Global Tipping Points Report 2025
publications.abstract: Global Tipping Points is led by Professor Tim Lenton from the University of Exeter with the support of more than 160 researchers from over 87 organisations in 23 countries. The report explores the governance of Earth system tipping points, associated risks, and how positive tipping points may be triggered to promote rapid, nonlinear change to a just and sustainable future. The report also includes four case studies of tipping points: the Amazon rainforest, Atlantic Ocean circulation, warm-water coral reefs and mountain glaciers: Áak'w T'áak Sít' (Mendenhall Glacier).

The report explores the governance of Earth system tipping points, associated risks, and how positive tipping points may be triggered to promote rapid, nonlinear change to a just and sustainable future. The report also includes four case studies of tipping points: the Amazon rainforest, Atlantic Ocean circulation, warm-water coral reefs and mountain glaciers: Áak'w T'áak Sít' (Mendenhall Glacier). The full report GTP Report 2025 can be accessed at: 10.5281/zenodo.18163977

publications.title: Identifying indicators of social-ecological adaptive capacity to forest disturbances in Europe
publications.abstract: Forest disturbances are intensifying across Europe, threatening ecosystem services and challenging forest management under global change. Despite the recognized importance of adaptive capacity of forests to natural disturbances, its assessment remains constrained by fragmented and often reductionist approaches. Here, we provide the first systematic social–ecological assessment of indicators of adaptive capacity to major forest disturbances (wind, insect outbreaks, and wildfires) across European forest systems. Using an anonymous expert questionnaire and a structured consensus workshop, we identified and prioritized indicators, assessed their spatial scales, and characterized their functional relationships with adaptive capacity. We identified 31 priority indicators spanning ecological and social domains. Most indicators were relevant across disturbance agents, although some were disturbance-specific. Ecological indicators primarily captured diversity, regeneration potential, and constraints such as herbivory, whereas social indicators reflected governance, socio-economic conditions, and infrastructure. Indicator–adaptive capacity relationships were frequently non-linear, with thresholds, saturation effects, and context-dependent responses. By moving beyond single-indicator approaches, this study provides a novel, structured framework to guide the selection of robust indicators and to define their relationships with adaptive capacity. Our findings highlight the need to integrate ecological and social dimensions and their interactions to support more comprehensive assessments of adaptive capacity to forest disturbances, informing forest management and policy under intensifying disturbance regimes.

publications.title: Climate Change and Reduction of Soil Organic Layer Thickness Increases Drought Risk in Mountain Forests of the Northern Alps
publications.abstract: ABSTRACT Background On ca. 10% of the forested sites in the Bavarian Alps (Germany) mountain, forest soils (so‐called folic histosols) are characterized by thick organic layers overlying poorly weathered calcareous parent material. Aim These organic layers play a critical role in releasing water and nutrients for vegetation, yet they are also sensitive to climate change, with warming‐induced increases in respiration potentially reducing their thickness and water‐holding capacity. Methods We used the process‐based water balance model LWF‐Brook90 to simulate soil water availability for 117 sites represented by georeferenced folic histosol profiles and to study the effect of different climate change scenarios (Representative Concentration Pathway [RCP] 2.6, 4.5, and 8.5) and humus loss (0%–75%) on the water balance. Specifically, we used high‐resolution climate data and HYPROP‐based Mualem–van Genuchten parameters to study potential changes in soil water retention and drought risk. Results Simulating the effects of changes in precipitation and temperature in combination with organic layer degradation and the resultant loss of water‐holding capacity led to significant increases in predicted transpiration deficits. A 50% reduction in organic layer thickness resulted in a distinct decrease of plant‐available moisture even under the optimistic RCP 2.6 scenario. Under severe climate change (scenario RCP 8.5) and 75% organic layer loss, water availability shifted up to two levels on a seven‐part relative scale of moisture regime. Although such extreme levels (>50%) of organic layer loss are unlikely under closed canopy conditions, they may occur following stand‐replacing disturbance events such as large‐scale windthrows or bark‐beetle outbreaks, which are expected to increase under climate change. Drought‐induced reductions of vegetation productivity may inhibit litter production and the replenishment of organic layers. Conclusion Our findings highlight the vulnerability of sites dominated by thick organic layers to climate‐driven water stress. By the end of the century, even under an optimistic scenario (no humus loss, RCP 4.5), the site water balance class on folic histosols is projected to decline by one class for the drier sites (75th percentile). Preventing a downward spiral of mountain forests triggered by climate change requires a holistic silvicultural concept for preserving folic histosols.

publications.title: Drivers of biodiversity across Central European forest reserves: reserve size, landscape context and habitat structure
publications.abstract: Abstract Protected areas play a central role in global forest biodiversity conservation. Improving their effectiveness needs informed site selection and management decisions - guided by robust ecological evidence. A better understanding is therefore needed how factors relevant for site selection affect biodiversity across taxonomic groups and forest types. Especially effects of reserve size and landscape context, as well as local habitat structures which are typically modified by management need to be better understood. To assess how reserve size, landscape forest share and local habitat characteristics – tree species composition, deadwood and tree-related microhabitats – influence biodiversity, we studied 44 protected forest areas of varying sizes across three major Central European forest types (riparian, upland and mountain forests). Within these reserves, we quantified coverage-based standardized diversity of beetles, spiders, birds and soil fungi. Biodiversity increased with reserve size for fungi, beetles and spiders. Increasing landscape-level forest share decreased beetle diversity. Interactive effects of reserve size and forest share were found for birds, indicating that diversity increased with reserve size more strongly in low-forested landscapes. Analysing forest specialists separately, we found no effects of reserve size and landscape-level forest share. The effect of local habitat characteristics varied across species groups and forest types. Beetle diversity was associated with deadwood volume and diversity, spider diversity with conifer share, canopy height variation and deadwood diversity, birds with canopy height variation and fungi with tree-related microhabitats. Overall, reserve size was the most consistent predictor of biodiversity across taxa, whereas landscape context and local habitat characteristics showed taxon- and forest-type-specific relationships. These findings suggest that forest conservation should aim at expanding the area under protection and promote structurally diverse habitats tailored to different taxonomic groups and forest types.

publications.title: Beneath the Surface: How the Declining Health of a Keystone Shrub Species Impacts Soil Carbon in a Temperate Mountain Ecosystem
publications.abstract: Abstract Mountain pine ( Pinus mugo Turra) is a key high-elevation species in the European Alps. It primarily establishes on exposed, erosion-prone sites and supports large soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks by sequestering carbon, stabilising soils, and preventing erosion. These functions are increasingly threatened as global change-related pressures like invasive pathogens impact mountain pine health. We investigated how declining mountain pine health affects SOC in Berchtesgaden National Park (BGNP), Germany. We studied two alternative vegetation states as potential outcomes of mountain pine decline, conifer-dominated forest and sparsely vegetated unstocked areas, and compared them to healthy and ailing mountain pine stands. We found that a transition from mountain pine to forest would have little effect on SOC ( p = 0.055). However, a trajectory to unstocked areas (with no woody plants establishing after mountain pine die-off) could result in 47.3% lower SOC compared to healthy mountain pine ( p < 0.001). To better understand the temporal development and landscape-scale consequences of such a potential loss of woody vegetation on areas currently stocked by mountain pine, we combined field data with carbon cycle simulations. Simulations showed that short-term SOC gains during mountain pine die-off shifted to long-term losses persisting over decades. A trajectory to unstocked areas on sites currently occupied by mountain pine could result in a loss of 28.3 kilotons of SOC for BGNP, whereof nearly 90% are in sensitive high elevation areas. We demonstrate that the global change-induced loss of a single keystone species could have long-lasting consequences on ecosystem functioning.

publications.title: A European database of comparable managed and unmanaged forest patches: the INFORMA Forest Management Platform
publications.abstract: Choices in forest management will be crucial to maintain our forests healthy in the next couple of decades, and to optimize the ecosystem services we can derive from them. The most fundamental choice is whether to manage the forest at all in the first place; are we better of intervening in our forests, and lending them a helping hand, or should be let them develop naturally and leave them unmanaged? Arguments can be made for either side, but they should be well-supported by empirical evidence. This European database of comparable managed and unmanaged forest patches - The INFORMA Forest Management Platform - has as a purpose to support research and policy in gathering this crucial evidence. The database has a specific, nested design to achieve this goal: comparable patches are linked together in 'clusters', in which patches are of similar forest types, have similar soil types, topographic contexts, climatic contexts and legacies. The database currently covers nine European countries, and contains over 12.000 hectares of forest. The database is a living database, and is continually updated. Request of not yet published or privacy-sensitive data can be submitted through https://ees.kuleuven.be/en/fnl/informa/. Similarly, submission of additional data and/or patches is facilitated through this site.

publications.title: Quantifying the contribution of cultivar parameter variation to uncertainty in future warming impacts on wheat yields across China's major winter wheat regions
Uncertainties in simulating wheat growth responses to waterlogging
publications.abstract: Waterlogging is an increasingly important stress in wheat growing regions, yet its representation in process based crop models (CMs) remains limited. We used a standardized AgMIP experiment to diagnose how 15 wheat CMs differ in their response to waterlogging timing, duration, and rainfall driven soil saturation. Before fitting waterlogging specific crop response coefficients to the eight waterlogged Lleida treatments in the current exercise, the ensemble median reproduced these treatments with an rRMSE of 17.0%. We interpret this as a pre fit extrapolative benchmark rather than strict independent validation because CMs retained their existing formulations and parameterizations and one CM reported prior calibration of soil water variables. Fitting waterlogging specific parameters to the same dataset reduced rRMSE to 6.3%, which is calibration goodness of fit rather than an independent test. Large differences among CMs remained when the calibrated parameters were transferred across phenological stages. Stem elongation was the single most frequently identified stage of maximum yield sensitivity, occurring in 4 of 15 CMs, although maxima occurred across all seven stages. Mean inter model variability in relative grain yield, expressed as the coefficient of variation across CMs, increased from 26.7% under 4 day waterlogging to 41.4% under 24 day waterlogging. A family balanced ensemble that first averaged related MONICA and SIMPLACE versions produced nearly identical mean responses (r = 0.998; maximum difference 2.8 %age points), indicating that related model versions did not drive the ensemble pattern. Most CMs showed weak yield responses to synthetic rainfall perturbations, including very large events, but these scenarios lack matched observations and therefore diagnose sensitivity rather than model bias. An exploratory structure response analysis found no single directly affected crop process that separated the severe stress response typologies. The strongest result is the large structural disagreement among current wheat CMs under standardized waterlogging perturbations, pointing to the combined importance of hydrological stress generation, crop process representation, parameterization, and development dependent damage and recovery for future model improvement.

publications.title: Generative Diffusion Outperforms Quantile Mapping for Climate Downscaling Across Scales
publications.abstract: Abstract Climate impact assessment at field and catchment scales depends on localised extremes, yet global climate models (~ 100 km) smooth over the terrain-driven variability, spatial structure, and inter-variable dependencies through which those extremes and compound events arise. Widely used statistical methods such as ISIMIP3BASD correct coarse-scale distributions but operate point-by-point, disrupting spatial coherence and daily co-variability. We present CasCorrDiff (Cascading Correction Diffusion), a generative diffusion framework that downscales in two supervised stages — 100 km to 10 km, then 10 km to 1 km — bridging a 100× resolution gap while preserving spatial covariance, inter-variable coupling, and physical event sequencing. Evaluated over Germany (2020–2024) against station and gridded references, CasCorrDiff outperforms ISIMIP3BASD and interpolated baselines in daily synchronisation (maximum temperature r = 0.99, NSE = 0.98) and reproduces observed mesoscale power spectra (10–200 km) and extreme indices, including the temperature Wasserstein distance (W = 0.37), consecutive dry days, and joint temperature–precipitation co-variability. It underestimates the 95th percentile of precipitation and loses skill in complex terrain. Because inference is decoupled from the multi-decade baselines that quantile mapping requires, a trained model downscales individual days on demand.

publications.title: Rising Indoor Wheat Yields in Vertical Farming
publications.abstract: ABSTRACT Wheat ( Triticum aestivum ) is central to human nutrition but increasingly challenged by climate change and resource constraints. Vertical farming offers a potential solution through controlled, year‐round cultivation, but the upper limits of productivity remain unclear. We conducted 39 climate chamber experiments (2022–2024) with electrical light and hydroponics, generating 719 yield datasets under varying light intensity, spectrum and photoperiod, carbon dioxide concentrations, air temperature, relative humidity, and hydroponic nutrient conditions. Robust K‐means analysis identified a grain yield cluster of 1.5 kg m −2 (15 t ha −1 ) per harvest derived from 2000 spikes m −2 , 52,000 grain m −2 , and 30 mg grain weight. The cluster was characterized by 4300 mol m −2 time‐integrated incident photosynthetic photon flux density per crop cycle, 1000 μmol mol −1 CO 2 , 23°C, and 59% relative humidity. Owing to the short crop cycle, 5.2 harvests are possible annually. Individual center‐positioned trays reached grain yields of 1.6 kg m −2 and grain weights up to 50 mg, indicating further yield potential. High grain numbers suggest no canopy‐level sink limitation, yet low grain weight under abundant resources indicates that neither source nor sink limitation alone fully explains yield performance. Instead, results suggest a possible source‐sink co‐limitation. This study establishes benchmarks for indoor wheat yields and novel insights into physiological constraints shaping yield potential in vertical farming.

publications.title: Modeling advection-driven cooling, humidification, and thermal stress effects of urban parks on adjacent built-up areas in a hot-humid city
Tree growth, physiology, and ecosystem services across a sealing gradient in Munich, Germany
publications.abstract: Urban trees provide essential ecosystem services, but impervious surface cover is associated with altered growing conditions and tree performance. We quantified mean imperviousness within a neighbourhood-scale 500 m buffer and classified 128 Acer platanoides , Robinia pseudoacacia , and Tilia cordata trees across the Munich–Freising region, Germany, into four categories: mostly unsealed (MU, <25%), partially sealed (PS, 25–49%), medium sealed (MS, 50–75%), and highly sealed (HS, >75%). Structural attributes, leaf physiology, local environmental conditions, and indicators of carbon storage, habitat provision, and surface-temperature reduction were assessed. Physiological measurements from two annual campaigns enabled interannual comparison but not assessment of intra-seasonal dynamics. Mean structural attributes did not differ significantly among sealing categories, although the explanatory strength of some allometric relationships varied descriptively across the gradient. Gas-exchange patterns differed descriptively among species, categories, and sampling campaigns; however, continuous imperviousness was not significantly associated with chlorophyll content (SPAD), transpiration, or stomatal conductance in the final models. Stomatal conductance was instead associated nonlinearly with shallow soil moisture and positively with precipitation and tree size. During physiological sampling, continuous imperviousness was positively associated with air temperature, corresponding to an estimated difference of approximately 0.20 °C per 10-percentage-point increase in imperviousness, whereas shallow soil moisture, relative humidity, and vapour pressure deficit showed no significant associations. Aboveground carbon storage was related primarily to DBH and species rather than sealing category; a 10% increase in DBH corresponded to an estimated 23.4% increase in carbon storage. Model-estimated microhabitat abundance was highest at partially sealed sites and was greatest for T. cordata . Model-adjusted surface-temperature reduction was descriptively higher over asphalt than over grass, although the surface materials were analysed separately; neither sealing category nor species was significantly associated with surface-temperature reduction over either surface material. Overall, neighbourhood-scale imperviousness was not a universally dominant predictor of urban-tree performance. Structural, physiological, and ecosystem-service patterns were associated with different combinations of species, tree size, sampling conditions, and local environmental characteristics. The findings support site- and service-specific urban-tree management while treating neighbourhood imperviousness as a contextual indicator rather than a direct measure of individual-tree growing conditions.

publications.title: Educator perspectives on the evolving competencies of urban forestry education
publications.abstract: Urban forestry has evolved into an increasingly distinct field of research, education, and professional practice that bridges ecological science, urban planning, governance, and community engagement. Despite the rapid expansion of urban forestry practice globally, there remains limited consensus regarding the core competencies and educational foundations required for urban forestry professionals. This study explores the knowledge areas, technical skills, and professional competencies considered essential for graduates entering the field. Our findings indicate that urban forestry education increasingly requires integration across disciplines. The study involved educators predominantly from North America, with additional participants from Europe and Australia. Key knowledge domains identified by participating educators include urban ecology, arboriculture, environmental science, ecosystem services, urban planning, and governance. Essential technical competencies include urban forest management, tree identification, GIS and spatial analysis, tree inventory methods, and ecosystem assessment. Cross-functional skills such as communication, community engagement, collaborative governance, leadership, and data interpretation, are also identified as important competencies. In this paper, we position urban forestry education as increasingly moving toward more integrated and context-responsive approaches capable of preparing graduates to address increasingly complex urban environmental and social challenges. This is in part due to the increasingly important societal role that urban forests play in e.g., urban climate adaptation, biodiversity conservation, and human health in urban policies and planning strategies. Strengthening interdisciplinary education and competency-based training will be critical to supporting the next generation of urban forestry professionals and advancing resilient, equitable, and sustainable urban forests.

publications.title: A hybrid deep learning framework for estimating urban tree transpiration
publications.abstract: Urban trees regulate urban water-energy exchange via transpiration, yet accurate estimates in urban settings remain challenging. Traditional Jarvis-type models often require frequent recalibration and can produce biased estimates when parameters vary or structural assumptions are violated. Alternatively, hybrid deep learning (DL) models that integrate data-driven approaches with process knowledge represent a promising alternative, merging the flexibility of DL with prior information from process models. Nonetheless, the effectiveness of these hybrids for estimating urban tree transpiration has rarely been evaluated. This study investigates three physics-guided DL strategies that incorporate the Jarvis model: residual learning (M2), weighted fusion (M3), and feature learning (M4), against three baselines: Jarvis, pure DL, and Random Forest (RF). We also analyze SHAP-based explainability to assess feature contributions and interactions. Utilizing observed hourly sap flow and environmental data from Munich and Würzburg (2015-2021), we estimate hourly latent heat flux ( 𝐿 ⁢ 𝐸 ) for two physiologically contrasting species, Tilia cordata and Robinia pseudoacacia , from shortwave radiation ( 𝑅 𝑠 ), air temperature ( 𝑇 𝑎 ), vapor pressure deficit ( 𝑉 ⁢ 𝑃 ⁢ 𝐷 ), soil moisture content ( 𝜃 ), and day of year ( 𝐷 ⁢ 𝑂 ⁢ 𝑌 ). All DL models outperform the Jarvis baseline, with M4 showing the best overall performance: test NSE 0.86 (0.90) and RMSE 11.43 (1.93) W/m 2 for two species, while maintaining strong performance with limited training data. SHAP identifies model-derived species-specific response patterns consistent with known differences in hydraulic architecture, and diagnoses regimes where Jarvis assumptions underperform. This framework offers a practical pathway for embedding process knowledge into broader urban evapotranspiration and microclimate models.
topics: Plant Water Relations and Carbon Dynamics

publications.title: Disentangling species-specific controls on urban tree transpiration: A Bayesian framework
publications.abstract: Urban trees regulate water-energy exchanges via transpiration. Although the Jarvis framework is widely used to describe plant physiological responses to environmental drivers, including vapor pressure deficit ( V P D ), solar radiation ( R s ), air temperature ( T a ), and soil moisture content ( θ ), key parameter and subfunction structural uncertainties remain insufficiently assessed at the species-specific level. Another challenge is modeling the transpiration variability across multiple sites and seasons simultaneously, particularly in climatically heterogeneous urban settings. Using hourly sap flux density ( S F D ) observations from nine urban sites in Munich and Würzburg, Germany (2015–2021), we fitted 81 subfunction configurations using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) Bayesian inference under uniform priors for two species with contrasting wood anatomy: diffuse-porous Tilia cordata and ring-porous Robinia pseudoacacia . Widely applicable information criterion (WAIC) based Sobol indices quantified structural sensitivity, and species-specific driver sensitivities were reconstructed under the best-performing structure. We then refitted the best Jarvis structure in a hierarchical Bayesian model, treating sites as random effects and adding a seasonal term. Results suggest that (i) at both the parameter and structure levels, the two species exhibit markedly different transpiration responses to environmental drivers, which can be interpreted in relation to known differences in hydraulic architecture and water-use strategy; (ii) model performance is sensitive to subfunction choice rather than increasing monotonically with structural complexity; and (iii) the hierarchical model captures cross-site variation in the transpiration upper bound and improves fit across sites and seasons, with the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) exceeding 80% for both species. Collectively, the framework provides uncertainty-aware, species-level Jarvis parameterizations at the single-tree scale, clarifies how species identity and model structure jointly shape sap flux dynamics, and offers an adaptable basis for interpreting and representing species-specific transpiration in urban microclimate models and urban forestry management.
topics: Plant Water Relations and Carbon Dynamics

publications.title: Dilepton Correlations from Heavy Flavor Decays
publications.abstract: Background: Azimuthal correlations between heavy flavor hadrons have been previously studied in $p+p$ collisions (Phys. Rev. C {\bf 98}, 034907 (2018), {\bf 101}, 034910 (2020)). These studies found good agreement with the data and provide a baseline for further studies in $p+A$ and $A+A$ collisions. Purpose: This work extends those studies to heavy flavor hadron decays to low mass lepton pairs. The low mass dilepton region is important for heavy ion collisions because of the interest in thermal dilepton production as a signature of the early time dynamics of the medium. Methods: Building on previous work, azimuthal correlations between leptons from semileptonic decays of heavy flavor hadrons are examined. The exclusive \textsc{HVQMNR} code is used in the calculations, made in the PHENIX acceptance at $\sqrt{s} = 200$~GeV and for dielectrons in ALICE at $\sqrt{s} = 13$~TeV. The $b \overline b$ decay contributions subtract like-sign lepton pairs from the opposite-sign signal. Results: The next-to-leading order calculations reproduce the trends of the PHENIX data. The calculations at 13~TeV show a change in signal as electron pair $p_T$ is increased, with the peak of the $Δϕ$ distribution moving from $Δϕ\sim π$ to $\sim 0$ and the contribution from bottom decays becoming dominant. The sensitivity of the signal to $k_T$ broadening is also studied and found to be small. Conclusions: It is found that the dependence on $k_T$ broadening previously observed is significantly reduced by the decay process. Despite this, the correlations between decay leptons retains some memory of the correlations between the parent hadrons in $p+p$ collisions. However, to study these correlations in heavy-ion collisions, it is necessary to separate them from thermal dilepton production in the same mass region.

publications.title: Corrigendum to “Search for a common baryon source in high-multiplicity pp collisions at the LHC” [Phys. Lett. B 811 (2020) 135849]
publications.abstract: In the original paper [1], the relative distance ⃗r∗ for p–p pairs composed of one primary and one secondary (i.e. coming from resonance decay) proton was not calculated correctly. Specifically, Eq. (5) in the original paper for the scenario in which one proton (proton 1) is primary and the other (proton 2) originates from a resonance decay should read ⃗ r∗ = ⃗r∗ core + ⃗s∗ res,2 , but it was implemented in the code used to extract the source core radius with a minus sign, namely ⃗r∗ = ⃗r∗ core − ⃗s∗ res,2 . The mistake was not present in the code used for the p–Λ results. The error leads to a reduction of the final total source size which hence required eventually a larger source core size to describe the measured p–p correlations in the different mT ranges. In Fig. 1 we present the original (left panel) and the updated (right panel) values of the rcore extracted from p–p correlations, compared with the published p–Λ results. The plot in the right panel of Fig. 1 replaces Fig. 5 in the original manuscript. The corrected numerical values are also available via HEPData [2]. The fitting procedure and the modelling of the resonances used for the updated results are the same as in the original paper, described respectively in Sec. 3 and Sec. 4 [1]. The net effect of the correction is a systematic shift, across all mT bins, of the rcore value for the p–p system of ∼ 0.09 fm. Considering the statistical and systematic uncertainties, the number of standard deviations (nσ) between the p–Λ (NLO13) and the corrected p–p results in the entire mT range is nσ =1.9. This value was obtained using the NLO13 p–Λ interaction from Ref. [3] for direct comparison with the results in the original manuscript. However, more recent studies on the source and the p–Λ interaction [4,5] have shown that the NLO parameterization [1,3] overestimates the spin-averaged scattering length by 10–15%. This implies that the extracted rcore for p–Λ (red points in Fig. 1) are biased towards larger radii. To address this, the p–Λ correlation functions in each mT bin have been re-fitted with an Usmani potential [6], fine-tuned to the eight best solutions listed in Table 1 of [5]. The best compatibility (nσ =0.90) between the p–p and p–Λ source sizes is achieved using point iv) from Table 1 in [5], which has scattering length (f) in the singlet (s) and triplet (t) channel of fs = 2.50 fm and ft = 1.32 fm. The corresponding mT scaling (red points) is plotted in the right panel of Fig. 2 and compared to the p–p results (blue band). These findings confirm the original message of the paper about the observation of a common mT scaling of the rcore for particle pairs in high-multiplicity pp collisions at center-of-mass energy √s=13TeV.
topics: Particle physics theoretical and experimental studies

publications.title: Jet modification via π 0 -hadron correlations in Au + Au collisions at s N N = 200 GeV
publications.abstract: High-momentum two-particle correlations are a useful tool for studying jet-quenching effects in the quark-gluon plasma. Angular correlations between neutral-pion triggers and charged hadrons with transverse momenta in the range 4--12 $\mathrm{GeV}/c$ and 0.5--7 $\mathrm{GeV}/c$, respectively, have been measured by the PHENIX experiment in 2014 for $\mathrm{Au}+\mathrm{Au}$ collisions at $\sqrt{{s}_{{}_{NN}}}=200$ GeV. Suppression is observed in the yield of high-momentum jet fragments opposite the trigger particle, which indicates jet suppression stemming from in-medium partonic energy loss, while enhancement is observed for low-momentum particles. The ratio and differences between the yield in $\mathrm{Au}+\mathrm{Au}$ collisions and $p+p$ collisions, ${I}_{AA}$ and ${\mathrm{\ensuremath{\Delta}}}_{AA}$, as a function of the trigger-hadron azimuthal separation, $\mathrm{\ensuremath{\Delta}}\ensuremath{\phi}$, are measured for the first time at the BNL Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider. These results better quantify how the yield of low-${p}_{T}$ associated hadrons is enhanced at wide angle, which is crucial for studying energy loss as well as medium-response effects.

publications.title: Zeolite-Confined Triatomic Cu Oxides at Silanol Nests as Hydrogen Transport Channels for H2 Production from Methanol Steam Reforming
publications.abstract: Abstract Cu-based catalysts offer high methanol steam reforming (MSR) activity but are limited by unstable Cu+–Cu0 interconversions due to the redox and sintering labilities of Cu. Herein, we developed a universal amino-functionalized “gripper” strategy for firmly and precisely anchoring atomically dispersed metals (e.g., Cu, Co, Ni) within Beta-zeolite. Triatomic Cu oxide (Cu3Ox) sites lower the methanol dehydrogenation activation barrier, and the synergistic interplay with adjacent OH groups from silanol nests accelerates H2 evolution and the MSR reaction. Spatially decoupling Cu-mediated methanol activation from silanol-driven H2 evolution at silanol nests as proton transport channels within the confining zeolite framework also effectively protected Cu from sintering, achieving a high specific activity of 951 molH2·molCu–1·h–1 and over 600 h of stability under continuous regeneration. This work provides a universal strategy for synthesizing atomically dispersed metal catalysts and a new design principle for maintaining the Cu structure during MSR.

publications.title: Charge heterogenized PtFe clusters defy activity–selectivity trade-offs in propane dehydrogenation
publications.abstract: Propane dehydrogenation is a pivotal industrial reaction, yet its efficiency is fundamentally constrained by the persistent scaling relation between propane activation and propylene desorption. Here, we transcend this compromise by deliberately constructing charge-state heterogeneity of silica-supported subnanometric PtFe clusters. Through synergistic Pt–Fe alloying and Pt–O–Fe interfacial bonding, we concurrently stabilize electron-rich (Ptδ−) and electron-deficient (Ptδ+) sites within a single catalytic ensemble. This architectural design enables the catalyst to achieve ~99% propylene selectivity at near-thermodynamic equilibrium conversion (~60% at 600 °C) with an ultralow Pt loading of 0.1 wt%, demonstrating high catalytic performance under reaction conditions. Mechanistic studies reveal that Ptδ− sites promote C–H bond cleavage via an electron-withdrawing effect that depletes σ-bond electron density, while neighboring Ptδ+ sites facilitate propylene desorption by modulating d–π orbital interactions. This work establishes charge-state heterogeneity as a versatile principle for circumventing scaling relations in catalytic alkane transformations. Propane dehydrogenation is a pivotal industrial reaction, yet its efficiency is fundamentally constrained by the persistent scaling relation between propane activation and propylene desorption. Here, the authors construct charge-state heterogeneity in silica supported subnanometric PtFe clusters.

publications.title: Remote allosteric control of single-atom Cu sites in Zr-MOFs enables selective CH 4 hydroxylation
publications.abstract: Highly selective oxidation of methane to liquid oxygenates under mild conditions remains challenging because of the difficulty in controlling overoxidation at highly reactive sites. Here, we demonstrate remote control of single-atom Cu reactivity through outer-shell coordination engineering in Zr-based metal-organic frameworks (MOFs). By anchoring Cu 1 to Zr-oxo nodes in UiO-66-X (X = -NO 2 , -H, and -CH 3 ), remote X-BDC ligands systematically modulate the electronic properties of Cu 1 sites and the catalytic microenvironment. In situ characterization combined with ab initio molecular dynamics in an explicitly solvated aqueous environment reveals a dynamic outer-shell-to-inner-shell regulation that reshapes the active structure and reactive oxygen species around Cu 1 sites, thereby facilitating CH 4 activation. In particular, the electron-withdrawing NO 2 -BDC ligand creates electron-deficient Cu 1 - • OH* sites, while adsorbed water further regulates active-site conformation. Consequently, Cu 1 /U6-NO 2 achieves a turnover frequency of 322.4 h −1 with nearly 100% oxygenate selectivity under mild conditions, establishing a general strategy for overcoming activity-selectivity trade-offs in methane conversion.

publications.title: How single-atom catalysis transformed from a nanoscience curiosity into a new paradigm for heterogeneous catalysis
Advances in Biological Electrolytic Water Splitting for Hydrogen Production
publications.abstract: Electrocatalytic water splitting stands as one of the most promising methods for producing clean and sustainable fuels from intermittent renewable energy sources. The strategic design of efficient electrocatalysts is crucial to achieving this goal. The versatility of hydrogen offers opportunities for large-scale, long-duration energy storage and industrial decarbonization. The term hydrogen carriers refers to molecules and materials capable of storing hydrogen at higher volumetric density than gaseous hydrogen. In the automotive sector, hydrogen can serve as a clean energy alternative to carbon-based fuels such as petroleum. However, the current practice of producing hydrogen from petroleum, coal, and natural gas is unsustainable. Utilizing solar energy, renewable hydrogen can be produced through processes such as pyrolysis, electrolysis, photolysis, and chemical decomposition of biomass. This article reviews the latest achievements and key milestones in the development of biomimetic catalysts in the field of water electrolysis. Compared to traditional catalysts, biomimetic electrocatalysts modeled on the structures of animals and plants exhibit unique surface wettability and efficient material/energy transfer characteristics. By leveraging the inherent structures and mechanisms of water enzymes and photosynthetic active sites according to specific application goals, the structure–activity relationship can be enhanced, thereby improving the electrochemical performance of enzyme-inspired catalysts in hydrogen and oxygen evolution reactions. In the field of water splitting, the most advanced biomimetic electrocatalysts have been developed through rational design, providing a blueprint for the next-generation hydrogen production platform.

publications.title: How Parenting Styles Shape Children’s Lifetime Outcomes
publications.abstract: This study examines how parenting styles predict children’s lifetime outcomes. Using a Swedish dataset which combines rich survey information on parenting styles with administrative records tracking children over five decades, we find that authoritarian parenting is negatively associated with children’s long-term success, especially regarding their educational attainment. The results for other parenting styles are more mixed. Authoritarian parenting remains a robust predictor of adverse outcomes even when accounting for ability and family background. We identify children’s knowledge accumulation and parental educational expectations as key mechanisms explaining these results.

Basic needs satisfaction as a fundamental distributive principle: Evidence from the lab and the field
publications.abstract: This paper provides clear evidence that concerns for basic needs satisfaction (BNS) represent a distinct distributional motive. Using a unified theoretical and experimental framework across five dictator-game experiments in Germany and Georgia (N=446), we disentangle BNS from motives such as maximin, selfishness, efficiency, generosity, and envy. A substantial share of participants displayed BNS-driven choices and were willing to forgo income and efficiency to satisfy others' basic needs. BNS remained robust across contexts, incentive schemes, and countries, and increased when needs satisfaction had strategic relevance. The results highlight the importance of BNS for understanding distributional preferences and policy design.

publications.title: The Global Variation in Risk and Time Preferences
publications.abstract: A growing body of empirical research has developed measures of economic preferences related to risk taking and intertemporal choice. This research has documented pronounced heterogeneity in preferences across and within societies, and also provided evidence that these differences are culturally transmitted. This chapter discusses existing data sets that allow for a comparable measurement across the globe, takes stock of commonalities and differences in approaches, and presents an extended synthetic cross-country data set that combines information from existing data sets. The analysis then establishes various empirical regularities, such as broadly similar patterns of heterogeneity across the globe, revealed by the different datasets, but also some systematic divergences by measurement approach, and substantial correlations of economic preferences with country-aggregate and individual-level outcomes and traits. We also briefly discuss international data sets measuring social preferences, and end with an outlook on avenues for future research.
